If the left depth of `root.right` equals `depth(root) - 1`, the entire left subtree is a full perfect tree of height `h-1` with `2^(h-1) - 1` nodes (plus the root gives `2^(h-1)`). If it's less, the bottom level hasn't reached the right subtree yet, meaning the right subtree is a full perfect tree of height `h-2`. In both cases, one subtree is fully solved in O(1) arithmetic, reducing the problem to a single branch recursive call.
count-complete-tree-nodes.approach:
Define a helper `get_depth(node)` that follows `node.left` down to a leaf and returns the height (1-indexed).
In `countNodes(root)`, handle the base case: if `root` is null, return 0.
Compute `h = get_depth(root)`.
If `h == 1`, return 1.
Compute `right_h = get_depth(root.right)`.
If `right_h == h - 1`: the left subtree is full. Add `(1 << (h - 1))` (left subtree + root) and recursively call `countNodes(root.right)`.
Else (`right_h == h - 2`): the right subtree is full at height `h - 2`. Add `(1 << (h - 2))` (right subtree + root) and recursively call `countNodes(root.left)`.

implement-queue-using-stacks.title: Implement Queue using Stacks
implement-queue-using-stacks.insight: Pouring elements from stack 1 to stack 2 reverses their order, turning LIFO into FIFO. If we leave them in stack 2 until stack 2 is completely empty, each element is moved exactly twice across its entire lifetime — once into stack 1 and once into stack 2 — yielding amortised O(1) time per operation.
implement-queue-using-stacks.approach:
Initialise two empty stacks: in_stack for pushes, and out_stack for pops and peeks.
Implement push(x) by appending x directly onto in_stack.
Write a private helper _shift() that moves all elements from in_stack to out_stack one by one, but ONLY if out_stack is currently empty.
Implement peek() by calling _shift(), then returning the top element of out_stack without removing it.
Implement pop() by calling _shift(), then popping and returning the top element of out_stack.
Implement empty() by returning true if both in_stack and out_stack are empty, false otherwise.

letter-case-permutation.title: Letter Case Permutation
letter-case-permutation.insight: Treat this as a decision tree where each character index is a level. Digits have a branching factor of 1, whereas alphabetic characters have a branching factor of 2 (lowercase and uppercase). By mutating a single character array in-place and snapshotting it at the leaves, we keep memory allocations to the bare minimum.
letter-case-permutation.approach:
Convert the input string s into a mutable list of characters to allow in-place modification.
Initialise an empty list 'res' to store the final valid strings.
Define a helper function 'backtrack(index)' that processes the string from left to right.
Base case: if index equals the length of the string, append the joined character list to 'res' and return.
Check if the character at 'index' is a letter or a digit.
If it's a digit, make a single recursive call: 'backtrack(index + 1)'.
If it's a letter, set it to lowercase, call 'backtrack(index + 1)', then set it to uppercase and call 'backtrack(index + 1)'.
Trigger the recursion with 'backtrack(0)' and return 'res'.

contiguous-array.title: Contiguous Array
contiguous-array.insight: If we map every 0 to -1 and leave 1 as +1, an equal count of 0s and 1s means a subarray sum of 0. A subarray sum from index i+1 to j is zero if and only if prefix_sum[j] == prefix_sum[i]. Therefore, we only need to store the earliest index where each running prefix sum first appeared; whenever we see that sum again, the distance from that first occurrence to the current index gives a valid candidate length.
contiguous-array.approach:
Initialise a running prefix sum counter to 0.
Initialise max_length to 0.
Create a hash map `seen` to store the earliest index for each prefix sum.
Seed the hash map with {0: -1} to correctly handle valid subarrays starting at index 0.
Iterate through the array with index `i` and value `x`.
Update prefix sum: add 1 if x == 1, else subtract 1.
If the current prefix sum is already in `seen`, calculate distance `i - seen[sum]` and update `max_length = max(max_length, distance)`.
If the current prefix sum is not in `seen`, record `seen[sum] = i`. (Do not overwrite if it already exists, as we want the earliest index).
Return `max_length` once the loop completes.

best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-iii.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock III
best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-iii.insight: At any day, you're in one of four financial positions: bought 1st stock, sold 1st stock, bought 2nd stock, or sold 2nd stock. Because each state only depends on the previous state's balance and today's price, you can collapse the DP table into just four variables updated sequentially in a single pass.
best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-iii.approach:
Initialise four variables: buy1 = -prices[0], sell1 = 0, buy2 = -prices[0], sell2 = 0.
Iterate through each price p in the prices array starting from index 0.
Update buy1 as max(buy1, -p), tracking the minimal spend for the first purchase.
Update sell1 as max(sell1, buy1 + p), tracking the maximum profit after selling the first stock.
Update buy2 as max(buy2, sell1 - p), reinvesting trade one's profit to minimise net spend on the second stock.
Update sell2 as max(sell2, buy2 + p), tracking the maximum total profit after closing both trades.
Notice that updating them in this order within the same iteration safely models same-day transitions without corrupting state.
Return sell2 at the end of the iteration.
best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-iii.solution:
class Solution:
    def maxProfit(self, prices: list[int]) -> int:
        if not prices:
            return 0
        
        # buy represents balance after buying (negative spend)
        # sell represents balance after selling (realised profit)
        buy1 = -prices[0]
        sell1 = 0
        buy2 = -prices[0]
        sell2 = 0
        
        for p in prices:
            buy1 = max(buy1, -p)
            sell1 = max(sell1, buy1 + p)
            buy2 = max(buy2, sell1 - p)
            sell2 = max(sell2, buy2 + p)
            
        return sell2

user-activity-for-the-past-30-days-i.title: User Activity for the Past 30 Days I
user-activity-for-the-past-30-days-i.insight: The problem simply requires bounded date filtering followed by a `COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)` grouped by date. In Pandas, that translates directly to a boolean mask for the date range, grouping by `activity_date`, and aggregating with `nunique()` on `user_id`.
user-activity-for-the-past-30-days-i.approach:
Identify the lower boundary: 29 days before 2019-07-27 gives 2019-06-28 inclusive.
Filter the DataFrame rows where `activity_date` falls between '2019-06-28' and '2019-07-27'.
Group the filtered records by `activity_date`.
Aggregate `user_id` using `nunique` to ensure users active multiple times on the same day are counted only once.
Reset the index to convert the grouped date back into a standard column.
Rename the columns to match the target schema: `day` and `active_users`.
Return the resulting DataFrame.
user-activity-for-the-past-30-days-i.solution:
import pandas as pd

def user_activity(activity: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    # 30-day window ending 2019-07-27 starts on 2019-06-28 inclusive
    mask = (activity['activity_date'] >= '2019-06-28') & (
        activity['activity_date'] <= '2019-07-27'
    )
    filtered = activity[mask]
    
    # Count distinct users per day
    df = (
        filtered.groupby('activity_date')['user_id']
        .nunique()
        .reset_index()
    )
    
    # Rename columns to match requested output schema
    df.columns = ['day', 'active_users']
    return df

stone-game-iv.title: Stone Game IV
stone-game-iv.insight: This is an impartial normal-play game. A state `i` is winning (`True`) if and only if there exists at least one integer `k >= 1` such that `i - k*k` is a losing state (`False`). If every reachable state from `i` is a winning state for the opponent, then state `i` is inevitably losing (`False`). We can compute this iteratively from 1 to n in O(n sqrt(n)) time.
stone-game-iv.approach:
1. Allocate a boolean DP array `dp` of size `n + 1`, initialised to `False`.
2. Base state: `dp[0] = False`, since having 0 stones means no valid move and an instant loss.
3. Loop `i` from 1 to `n` to determine the outcome for a pile of size `i`.
4. For each `i`, iterate through all square steps `k * k <= i` starting from `k = 1`.
5. Check if `dp[i - k * k]` is `False` (meaning the opponent would lose from that state).
6. If a `False` transition is found, mark `dp[i] = True` and break early out of the inner loop.
7. If the inner loop finishes without finding any losing transition, `dp[i]` remains `False`.
8. Return `dp[n]` as the final answer for Alice.

counting-bits.title: Counting Bits
counting-bits.insight: Every integer i is just i >> 1 (which has already been processed) shifted left by one, plus whatever sits at the lowest bit (i & 1). Therefore, ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1). Alternatively, ans[i] = ans[i & (i - 1)] + 1, clearing the lowest set bit.
counting-bits.approach:
Allocate an integer array 'ans' of size n + 1 initialised to 0.
Set the base case ans[0] = 0, which is naturally handled by zero-initialisation.
Loop i from 1 up to n inclusive.
For each i, compute ans[i] using the relation: ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1).
Since i >> 1 < i, ans[i >> 1] is guaranteed to be solved already.
Return the populated ans array.

longest-substring-of-one-repeating-chara.title: Longest Substring of One Repeating Character
longest-substring-of-one-repeating-chara.insight: Every single-character update only affects an O(log n) path in a segment tree. To stitch two adjacent segments L and R in O(1), we only need five values per node: the max run inside, prefix run length, suffix run length, left boundary character, and right boundary character. When L's rightmost character equals R's leftmost character, their adjacent suffix and prefix seamlessly merge across the boundary.
longest-substring-of-one-repeating-chara.approach:
1. Allocate flat arrays of size 4n for the segment tree attributes: max_len, pref_len, suff_len, first_char, and last_char.
2. Implement a push_up(node, left_sz, right_sz) helper that merges node's two children (2*node and 2*node+1).
3. In push_up, initialise node's max_len as max(L.max_len, R.max_len), first_char as L.first_char, and last_char as R.last_char.
4. If L.last_char == R.first_char, candidate cross-boundary length is L.suff_len + R.pref_len; update max_len with this.
5. Set pref_len to L.pref_len, but if L is entirely uniform (L.pref_len == left_sz) and boundary chars match, extend it by R.pref_len.
6. Symmetrically calculate suff_len using R and L.
7. Build the segment tree recursively in O(n) from s.
8. For each query, execute a point update on the segment tree in O(log n), then read root's max_len (tree index 1) into the result list.
longest-substring-of-one-repeating-chara.solution:
class Solution:
    def longestRepeating(self, s: str, queryCharacters: str, queryIndices: list[int]) -> list[int]:
        n = len(s)
        # 4 * n is sufficient space for a standard binary segment tree
        max_len = [0] * (4 * n)
        pref = [0] * (4 * n)
        suff = [0] * (4 * n)
        first_ch = [''] * (4 * n)
        last_ch = [''] * (4 * n)

        def push_up(node: int, left_len: int, right_len: int) -> None:
            l, r = 2 * node, 2 * node + 1
            first_ch[node] = first_ch[l]
            last_ch[node] = last_ch[r]
            
            # Base best inside either child
            best = max(max_len[l], max_len[r])
            p = pref[l]
            s_len = suff[r]

            # If boundary characters match, merge across midpoint
            if last_ch[l] == first_ch[r]:
                best = max(best, suff[l] + pref[r])
                if pref[l] == left_len:
                    p = left_len + pref[r]
                if suff[r] == right_len:
                    s_len = right_len + suff[l]

            max_len[node] = best
            pref[node] = p
            suff[node] = s_len

        def build(node: int, l: int, r: int) -> None:
            if l == r:
                ch = s[l]
                max_len[node] = pref[node] = suff[node] = 1
                first_ch[node] = last_ch[node] = ch
                return
            mid = (l + r) // 2
            build(2 * node, l, mid)
            build(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r)
            push_up(node, mid - l + 1, r - mid)

        def update(node: int, l: int, r: int, idx: int, ch: str) -> None:
            if l == r:
                first_ch[node] = last_ch[node] = ch
                return
            mid = (l + r) // 2
            if idx <= mid:
                update(2 * node, l, mid, idx, ch)
            else:
                update(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, idx, ch)
            push_up(node, mid - l + 1, r - mid)

        build(1, 0, n - 1)
        ans = []
        for ch, idx in zip(queryCharacters, queryIndices):
            update(1, 0, n - 1, idx, ch)
            ans.append(max_len[1])
        
        return ans

water-bottles.title: Water Bottles
water-bottles.insight: Think about the net cost of one exchange. Handing in numExchange empties gives you 1 full bottle, which produces 1 empty bottle once drunk. That means each extra drink costs you exactly numExchange - 1 empties net. Because you cannot sacrifice the very last empty bottle (you need it to actually hold a drink), you have numBottles - 1 spare empties to burn across transactions.
water-bottles.approach:
1. Start by accounting for the initial drinks: you drink all numBottles initially.
2. Identify the net empty bottle cost per exchange: each exchange yields 1 new bottle for numExchange empties, net cost is numExchange - 1.
3. Determine the disposable empty bottles: you must always retain at least 1 empty bottle at the end, leaving numBottles - 1 empties to trade away.
4. Compute additional drinks via integer division: (numBottles - 1) // (numExchange - 1).
5. Sum the initial drinks and the additional drinks obtained.
6. Return the total sum directly.

maximum-length-substring-with-two-occurr.title: Maximum Length Substring With Two Occurrences
maximum-length-substring-with-two-occurr.insight: Since valid substrings have contiguous indices and character counts monotonically increase as we expand, a two-pointer sliding window guarantees that each character enters and exits the window at most once. Whenever introducing s[right] violates the rule (count becomes 3), incrementing left until s[right]'s count is reduced back to 2 restores the invariant in amortised O(1) time.
maximum-length-substring-with-two-occurr.approach:
Initialise left pointer `left = 0`, a max length variable `max_len = 0`, and a frequency map or array of size 26.
Iterate the right pointer `right` from 0 to len(s) - 1.
Increment the frequency of character `s[right]`.
While the frequency of `s[right]` is strictly greater than 2, decrement the frequency of `s[left]` and advance `left` by 1.
Once the window is valid again, update `max_len = max(max_len, right - left + 1)`.
Return `max_len` after the loop finishes.

employee-free-time.title: Employee Free Time
employee-free-time.insight: Because each employee's own intervals are already sorted, this is identical to merging K sorted lists. We maintain a min-heap of size K holding the earliest unprocessed interval from each employee. As we pop the next earliest interval, if its start is greater than the running `prev_end`, we have found a common gap `[prev_end, curr.start]`; otherwise, we just stretch `prev_end = max(prev_end, curr.end)`.
employee-free-time.approach:
Initialise an empty min-heap and a result list `free_time`.
Push the first interval of each employee into the heap as `(interval.start, emp_idx, interval_idx)`.
Pop the smallest element; set `prev_end = interval.end`, and if that employee has a next interval, push it onto the heap.
While the heap is non-empty, pop the next interval `(start, emp_idx, idx)`.
If `start > prev_end`, record `Interval(prev_end, start)` into `free_time` because no employee is working during this window.
Update `prev_end = max(prev_end, end)` to extend the current merged working block.
If this employee has a subsequent interval, push `(schedule[emp_idx][idx + 1].start, emp_idx, idx + 1)` into the heap.
Return `free_time` once the heap is exhausted.
employee-free-time.solution:
import heapq

# Definition for an Interval.
# class Interval:
#     def __init__(self, start: int = None, end: int = None):
#         self.start = start
#         self.end = end

class Solution:
    def employeeFreeTime(self, schedule: 'list[list[Interval]]') -> 'list[Interval]':
        pq = []
        # Seed min-heap with the first interval of each employee
        for emp_idx, emp_intervals in enumerate(schedule):
            if emp_intervals:
                pq.append((emp_intervals[0].start, emp_idx, 0))
        heapq.heapify(pq)
        
        if not pq:
            return []
        
        # Initialise running boundary with the earliest interval
        _, emp_idx, int_idx = heapq.heappop(pq)
        first_int = schedule[emp_idx][int_idx]
        prev_end = first_int.end
        if int_idx + 1 < len(schedule[emp_idx]):
            heapq.heappush(pq, (schedule[emp_idx][int_idx + 1].start, emp_idx, int_idx + 1))
            
        res = []
        while pq:
            _, emp_idx, int_idx = heapq.heappop(pq)
            curr = schedule[emp_idx][int_idx]
            
            # If there's a disjoint gap between prev_end and curr.start
            if curr.start > prev_end:
                res.append(Interval(prev_end, curr.start))
                prev_end = curr.end
            else:
                prev_end = max(prev_end, curr.end)
                
            if int_idx + 1 < len(schedule[emp_idx]):
                heapq.heappush(pq, (schedule[emp_idx][int_idx + 1].start, emp_idx, int_idx + 1))
                
        return res

lowest-common-ancestor-of-a-binary-searc.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree
lowest-common-ancestor-of-a-binary-searc.insight: In a BST, all values in the left subtree are strictly smaller than the current node, and all in the right are strictly larger. As long as both p and q are on the same side of the current node, their LCA must also lie on that side; the very first node where p and q diverge—or where the current node matches p or q—is guaranteed to be the LCA.
lowest-common-ancestor-of-a-binary-searc.approach:
1. Start a pointer `curr` at the root of the BST.
2. Enter a while loop that continues whilst `curr` is not null.
3. Check if both `p.val` and `q.val` are strictly smaller than `curr.val`.
4. If so, both targets are in the left subtree, so update `curr = curr.left`.
5. Check if both `p.val` and `q.val` are strictly greater than `curr.val`.
6. If so, both targets are in the right subtree, so update `curr = curr.right`.
7. If neither condition holds, we have reached the split point (or `curr` is `p` or `q`), so return `curr` immediately.

gas-station.title: Gas Station
gas-station.insight: Two key mathematical insights unlock O(n). First, if sum(gas) < sum(cost), it's physically impossible to complete the circuit from anywhere. Second, if you start at station A and run out of gas trying to reach station B + 1, no station between A and B can be the start either — because you arrived at those intermediate stations with non-negative surplus gas, so starting from them with 0 gas would fail even earlier. Therefore, the next possible start is immediately B + 1.
gas-station.approach:
Initialize three variables: total_tank = 0, curr_tank = 0, and start_idx = 0.
Iterate through the stations from index 0 to n - 1.
At station i, calculate the net gain: diff = gas[i] - cost[i].
Add diff to both total_tank and curr_tank.
Check if curr_tank is less than 0.
If curr_tank < 0, reset start_idx to i + 1 and curr_tank to 0.
After finishing the loop, check if total_tank >= 0.
If total_tank >= 0, return start_idx; otherwise, return -1.
gas-station.solution:
class Solution:
    def canCompleteCircuit(self, gas: list[int], cost: list[int]) -> int:
        total_tank = 0
        curr_tank = 0
        start_idx = 0
        
        for i in range(len(gas)):
            gain = gas[i] - cost[i]
            total_tank += gain
            curr_tank += gain
            
            # If we cannot reach the next station, reset start candidate
            if curr_tank < 0:
                start_idx = i + 1
                curr_tank = 0
                
        return start_idx if total_tank >= 0 else -1

confirmation-rate.title: Confirmation Rate
confirmation-rate.insight: In SQL, taking the `AVG()` of a conditional expression `action = 'confirmed'` directly computes `(count of confirmed) / (total count)` in a single pass. A `LEFT JOIN` ensures users with zero confirmation requests are preserved, producing `NULL` for `action`, which `AVG()` evaluates to `NULL` — meaning `IFNULL(ROUND(AVG(...), 2), 0.00)` handles all cases cleanly without explicit denominators or division-by-zero checks.
confirmation-rate.approach:
1. Start with `Signups s` on the left side to retain every registered user.
2. Perform a `LEFT JOIN` with `Confirmations c` on `s.user_id = c.user_id`.
3. Group the joined rows by `s.user_id` so each user produces exactly one output row.
4. In the `SELECT` clause, project `s.user_id`.
5. Use `CASE WHEN c.action = 'confirmed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END` (or `c.action = 'confirmed'`) inside `AVG()` to calculate the ratio.
6. Wrap the `AVG()` in `ROUND(..., 2)` to format to two decimal places.
7. Wrap the rounded value in `IFNULL(..., 0.00)` (or `COALESCE`) so users with zero requests (where `AVG` evaluates over all `NULL`s) output `0.00`.
8. Alias the aggregated column as `confirmation_rate` and return.
confirmation-rate.time: O(N + M log N) where N is rows in Signups and M is rows in Confirmations
confirmation-rate.space: O(N + M) space required by the query planner to materialize the hash join / grouped aggregation buffers before emitting output rows
confirmation-rate.solution:
import pandas as pd

def confirmation_rate(signups: pd.DataFrame, confirmations: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    # Left merge to keep all signups
    merged = pd.merge(signups[['user_id']], confirmations, on='user_id', how='left')
    
    # Map 'confirmed' to 1, 'timeout' to 0; NULL remains NaN
    merged['is_confirmed'] = merged['action'].apply(lambda x: 1.0 if x == 'confirmed' else (0.0 if x == 'timeout' else None))
    
    # Group by user_id and take mean, filling NaN (no requests) with 0.0
    result = merged.groupby('user_id')['is_confirmed'].mean().fillna(0.0).round(2).reset_index()
    result.rename(columns={'is_confirmed': 'confirmation_rate'}, inplace=True)
    
    return result

longest-continuous-subarray-with-absolut.title: Longest Continuous Subarray With Absolute Diff Less Than or Equal to Limit
longest-continuous-subarray-with-absolut.insight: The condition 'absolute difference between any two elements is at most limit' is strictly equivalent to 'max(subarray) - min(subarray) <= limit'. A standard sliding window works because expanding right only ever increases or keeps the spread equal, and shrinking left reduces or maintains it. To achieve O(N) rather than O(N log N), we maintain two monotonic deques: one strictly decreasing (front holds window maximum) and one strictly increasing (front holds window minimum).
longest-continuous-subarray-with-absolut.approach:
1. Initialise two double-ended queues: max_dq (monotonically decreasing) and min_dq (monotonically increasing).
2. Initialise two pointers: left = 0 and max_len = 0.
3. Iterate right from 0 through len(nums) - 1 with current value val = nums[right].
4. Maintain max_dq: while max_dq is not empty and its back element is strictly less than val, pop from the back.
5. Maintain min_dq: while min_dq is not empty and its back element is strictly greater than val, pop from the back.
6. Push val to the back of both max_dq and min_dq.
7. While max_dq.front - min_dq.front > limit, check if nums[left] matches max_dq.front (pop front if so) and if it matches min_dq.front (pop front if so), then increment left.
8. Update max_len with right - left + 1 at the end of each iteration.
9. Return max_len once the loop finishes.

maximum-number-of-vowels-in-a-substring-.title: Maximum Number of Vowels in a Substring of Given Length
maximum-number-of-vowels-in-a-substring-.insight: Adjacent windows of size k share k - 1 characters. When sliding the window one position to the right, we only need to adjust the count: +1 if the incoming character s[i] is a vowel, and -1 if the outgoing character s[i - k] was a vowel.
maximum-number-of-vowels-in-a-substring-.approach:
Define a lookup set `vowels = {'a', 'e', 'i', 'o', 'u'}` for O(1) membership checks.
Count vowels in the prefix window `s[0:k]` to initialise `curr_vowels`.
Set `max_vowels = curr_vowels`.
If `max_vowels == k`, early return `k` since we cannot beat this upper bound.
Iterate an index `i` from `k` up to `len(s) - 1`.
If `s[i]` is in `vowels`, increment `curr_vowels` by 1 (new element in).
If `s[i - k]` is in `vowels`, decrement `curr_vowels` by 1 (old element out).
Update `max_vowels = max(max_vowels, curr_vowels)` and return `k` immediately if `max_vowels == k`.
Return `max_vowels` after the loop finishes.

fibonacci-number.title: Fibonacci Number
fibonacci-number.insight: Notice that to compute F(i), we only ever need F(i-1) and F(i-2). We don't need to maintain an entire array of historical values; keeping two rolling variables reduces memory usage from O(n) down to O(1).
fibonacci-number.approach:
Check if n is 0 or 1; if so, return n directly as the base case.
Initialise two pointers or scalar variables: prev2 = 0 (representing F(0)) and prev1 = 1 (representing F(1)).
Loop from index 2 up to n inclusive.
In each iteration, calculate current = prev1 + prev2.
Shift the window forward: set prev2 = prev1, then prev1 = current.
After the loop finishes, return prev1 as F(n).

find-all-numbers-disappeared-in-an-array.title: Find All Numbers Disappeared in an Array
find-all-numbers-disappeared-in-an-array.insight: Every value is in [1, n], which perfectly matches the 0-indexed bounds [0, n - 1]. We can repurpose the sign bit of nums[abs(x) - 1] as a boolean flag to indicate we've seen number x, without losing the original magnitude of the data.
find-all-numbers-disappeared-in-an-array.approach:
Iterate through the array from index 0 to n - 1.
For each element, take its absolute value val = abs(nums[i]).
Calculate its target 0-based index: target = val - 1.
If nums[target] is positive, flip its sign to negative to mark val as present.
If nums[target] is already negative, do nothing because we've encountered a duplicate.
Perform a second pass from index 0 to n - 1.
If nums[i] remains positive, it means value i + 1 was never marked, so append i + 1 to the result list.
Return the collected result list.

insert-interval.title: Insert Interval
insert-interval.insight: Because intervals are already sorted and disjoint, any overlap with newInterval forms a single contiguous subsegment. This means we can process the list in exactly three linear stages without sorting: before overlap, during overlap, and after overlap.
insert-interval.approach:
Initialise an empty result list and an index pointer i = 0.
Phase 1 (Left): Whilst i < len(intervals) and intervals[i].end < newInterval.start, append intervals[i] directly to result.
Phase 2 (Merge): Whilst i < len(intervals) and intervals[i].start <= newInterval.end, expand newInterval by setting newInterval.start = min(newInterval.start, intervals[i].start) and newInterval.end = max(newInterval.end, intervals[i].end), incrementing i at each step.
Append the newly merged newInterval to result.
Phase 3 (Right): Whilst i < len(intervals), append all remaining intervals[i] directly to result.
Return the result list.
insert-interval.solution:
class Solution:
    def insert(self, intervals: list[list[int]], newInterval: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
        result = []
        i = 0
        n = len(intervals)
        
        # Phase 1: Add all intervals ending before newInterval starts
        while i < n and intervals[i][1] < newInterval[0]:
            result.append(intervals[i])
            i += 1
            
        # Phase 2: Merge overlapping intervals into newInterval
        while i < n and intervals[i][0] <= newInterval[1]:
            newInterval[0] = min(newInterval[0], intervals[i][0])
            newInterval[1] = max(newInterval[1], intervals[i][1])
            i += 1
        result.append(newInterval)
        
        # Phase 3: Add all remaining intervals
        while i < n:
            result.append(intervals[i])
            i += 1
            
        return result

employee-bonus.title: Employee Bonus
employee-bonus.insight: An INNER JOIN drops employees who never received a bonus because their empId isn't in the Bonus table. A LEFT JOIN keeps all employees, turning missing bonus rows into NULL, so we simply check `bonus < 1000 OR bonus IS NULL` — remembering that in SQL, standard comparisons like `< 1000` evaluate to UNKNOWN (not TRUE) on NULL values.
employee-bonus.approach:
Start from the Employee table aliased as `e`.
Perform a `LEFT JOIN` on the Bonus table aliased as `b` matching on `e.empId = b.empId`.
In the `WHERE` clause, add the condition `b.bonus < 1000 OR b.bonus IS NULL`.
Select the required columns `e.name` and `b.bonus`.
In Pandas/Python: merge `employee` and `bonus` on `empId` using `how='left'`.
Filter rows where `bonus < 1000` or `bonus.isna()`.
Return only `[['name', 'bonus']]`.
employee-bonus.solution:
import pandas as pd

def employee_bonus(employee: pd.DataFrame, bonus: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    # Left merge to retain all employees even without a bonus record
    merged = employee.merge(bonus, on='empId', how='left')
    
    # Filter for bonus < 1000 or missing bonus (NaN)
    result = merged[(merged['bonus'] < 1000) | (merged['bonus'].isna())]
    
    # Project only the requested columns
    return result[['name', 'bonus']]

# SQL Equivalent:
# SELECT e.name, b.bonus
# FROM Employee e
# LEFT JOIN Bonus b ON e.empId = b.empId
# WHERE b.bonus < 1000 OR b.bonus IS NULL;

reverse-vowels-of-a-string.title: Reverse Vowels of a String
reverse-vowels-of-a-string.insight: Because string reversal is symmetrical, we can use two pointers starting at opposite ends. We advance both pointers inward until both land on vowels, swap them, and repeat until they cross.
reverse-vowels-of-a-string.approach:
1. Define a hash set of vowels containing both lowercase and uppercase 'aeiouAEIOU' for O(1) lookups.
2. Convert the input string s into a list of characters since Python strings are immutable.
3. Initialise two pointers: left = 0 and right = len(s) - 1.
4. Enter a while loop that runs while left < right.
5. Increment left while left < right and chars[left] is not a vowel.
6. Decrement right while left < right and chars[right] is not a vowel.
7. Swap chars[left] and chars[right], then advance left by 1 and decrement right by 1.
8. Join the character list back into a string and return it.

subsets-ii.title: Subsets II
subsets-ii.insight: By sorting the array, identical values are grouped together. At any recursion depth starting from index 'start', if `nums[i] == nums[i-1]` and `i > start`, picking `nums[i]` would explore the exact same subtree as picking `nums[i-1]`. Skipping that iteration prunes all duplicate branches before they start.
subsets-ii.approach:
1. Sort the input array `nums` in ascending order so duplicate numbers are adjacent.
2. Initialise an empty results list `res` to hold all unique subsets.
3. Define a helper function `backtrack(start, path)` that builds subsets.
4. Append a copy of `path` to `res` at the start of every call (since every intermediate path is a valid subset).
5. Iterate through candidate indices `i` from `start` to `len(nums) - 1`.
6. Check if `i > start` and `nums[i] == nums[i-1]`; if true, `continue` to skip the duplicate.
7. Append `nums[i]` to `path`, make the recursive call `backtrack(i + 1, path)`, and then pop `nums[i]` to backtrack.
8. Call `backtrack(0, [])` and return `res`.

count-good-numbers.title: Count Good Numbers
count-good-numbers.insight: Each position is completely independent: even index positions always have 5 valid choices, and odd index positions always have 4 valid choices. For length n, there are ceil(n/2) even indices and floor(n/2) odd indices, giving a total of 5^((n+1)/2) * 4^(n/2). Because n <= 10^15, we compute both powers in O(log n) using binary exponentiation modulo 10^9 + 7.
count-good-numbers.approach:
1. Define the modulus MOD = 1_000_000_007.
2. Calculate the number of even indices as (n + 1) // 2.
3. Calculate the number of odd indices as n // 2.
4. Implement a helper for modular binary exponentiation: pow_mod(base, exp, mod).
5. Inside the helper, initialize result = 1, base = base % mod.
6. While exp > 0, if exp is odd, multiply result by base (modulo mod).
7. Square base (modulo mod) and halve exp with integer division.
8. Compute (pow_mod(5, even_count, MOD) * pow_mod(4, odd_count, MOD)) % MOD and return it.
count-good-numbers.solution:
class Solution:
    def countGoodNumbers(self, n: int) -> int:
        MOD = 10**9 + 7
        
        # Built-in pow supports efficient O(log n) modular exponentiation
        even_count = (n + 1) // 2
        odd_count = n // 2
        
        ans = (pow(5, even_count, MOD) * pow(4, odd_count, MOD)) % MOD
        return ans

rearrange-array-elements-by-sign.title: Rearrange Array Elements by Sign
rearrange-array-elements-by-sign.insight: All positive numbers belong at even indices (0, 2, 4, ...) and all negative numbers belong at odd indices (1, 3, 5, ...), in their original relative order. Because their destination indices are disjoint and strictly increasing, we can pre-allocate the output array and write directly into it with two running pointers (`pos_idx = 0`, `neg_idx = 1`) as we stream through `nums`.
rearrange-array-elements-by-sign.approach:
1. Determine the length `n` of `nums` and initialise a result list `ans` of size `n` with dummy zeros.
2. Initialise `pos_idx = 0` to track the next available even index for positive numbers.
3. Initialise `neg_idx = 1` to track the next available odd index for negative numbers.
4. Iterate through each integer `x` in `nums` sequentially.
5. If `x > 0`, write `x` to `ans[pos_idx]` and increment `pos_idx` by 2.
6. If `x < 0`, write `x` to `ans[neg_idx]` and increment `neg_idx` by 2.
7. Return `ans` once the loop completes.

swap-nodes-in-pairs.title: Swap Nodes in Pairs
swap-nodes-in-pairs.insight: To swap two adjacent nodes, say A and B, you need access to the node preceding A. By introducing a dummy sentinel node before the head, the head pair is treated identically to any subsequent pair: we point prev.next to B, A.next to B.next, and B.next to A, then advance prev to A.
swap-nodes-in-pairs.approach:
1. Initialise a dummy `ListNode(0)` whose `next` points to `head`.
2. Set a pointer `prev` to the dummy node.
3. Enter a while loop that runs as long as `prev.next` and `prev.next.next` exist.
4. Identify the two nodes to swap: `first = prev.next` and `second = prev.next.next`.
5. Rewire pointers: set `first.next = second.next`, then `second.next = first`, then `prev.next = second`.
6. Advance `prev` to `first`, which is now the second node in the processed pair.
7. Return `dummy.next` as the new head of the list.
swap-nodes-in-pairs.solution:
# Definition for singly-linked list.
# class ListNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.next = next

class Solution:
    def swapPairs(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        # Sentinel node to cleanly handle edge cases at head
        dummy = ListNode(0, head)
        prev = dummy
        
        # Loop while there is at least one full pair left to swap
        while prev.next and prev.next.next:
            first = prev.next
            second = prev.next.next
            
            # Execute the 3-pointer swap
            first.next = second.next
            second.next = first
            prev.next = second
            
            # Move prev to the end of the newly swapped pair
            prev = first
            
        return dummy.next

bus-routes.title: Bus Routes
bus-routes.insight: Instead of connecting stops to stops, connect stops to buses. By maintaining an inverted index of stop -> list of bus IDs, our BFS queue only needs to expand each bus route once. Once a bus is boarded, all its stops are reached at the current bus count, and we mark the entire bus as visited so we never scan its stops again.
bus-routes.approach:
Check base case: if source == target, return 0 straight away.
Build a hash map stop_to_routes mapping each stop ID to a list of bus route indices that visit it.
If source is not in stop_to_routes, return -1 immediately.
Initialise a queue with source, a visited_stops set with source, and an empty visited_routes set.
Initialise bus_count to 0 and loop whilst the queue is not empty.
For each level (all stops currently in the queue), increment bus_count by 1.
Pop a stop, iterate through all route indices serving this stop.
Skip routes already in visited_routes; otherwise add the route to visited_routes.
For every stop in this route: if it equals target, return bus_count; if unvisited, mark it and push to the queue.
If the queue empties without finding target, return -1.
bus-routes.time: O(N + sum(L_i)) where N is the number of routes and L_i is the number of stops in route i
bus-routes.space: O(sum(L_i)) for storing the stop-to-route adjacency hash map and visited sets

cheapest-flights-within-k-stops.title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
cheapest-flights-within-k-stops.insight: Standard shortest path algorithms don't naturally constrain edge count, but Bellman-Ford inherently computes the shortest path of at most i edges on iteration i. If we run Bellman-Ford for k + 1 rounds and strictly use distances from round i-1 to compute round i (avoiding within-round cascading updates), dist[dst] gives the exact minimum cost using at most k stops.
cheapest-flights-within-k-stops.approach:
Initialise an array `dist` of size `n` with infinity, setting `dist[src] = 0`.
Loop `k + 1` times, where each iteration represents allowing one additional flight hop.
Create a shallow copy `temp = dist[:]` at the start of each iteration to prevent updating and reusing values within the same step.
Iterate through every flight `(u, v, cost)` in `flights`.
If `dist[u]` is not infinity and `dist[u] + cost < temp[v]`, update `temp[v] = dist[u] + cost`.
Assign `dist = temp` at the end of the outer loop iteration.
After all `k + 1` rounds, return `dist[dst]` if it is not infinity, otherwise return `-1`.

implement-trie-prefix-tree.title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
implement-trie-prefix-tree.insight: By sharing common prefixes in a tree structure where each node represents a character, branching on at most 26 children, both full-word search and prefix matching reduce to a straightforward path traversal taking strictly O(L) time.
implement-trie-prefix-tree.approach:
Define an inner `TrieNode` containing a fixed array/map of size 26 for children and a boolean `is_end` flag initialised to false.
Initialise the `Trie` with a dummy `root` node.
For `insert(word)`: start at `root`, iterate through each character, compute index `c - 'a'`, create a new `TrieNode` if the child pointer is null, and advance the current pointer. Mark the final node's `is_end` as true.
Create a helper `_find(prefix)` that traverses the tree matching characters: returns the node at the end of the prefix, or null if any character branch is missing.
For `search(word)`: call `_find(word)`. Return true if the returned node is not null AND its `is_end` flag is true.
For `startsWith(prefix)`: call `_find(prefix)`. Return true if the returned node is not null.
implement-trie-prefix-tree.time: O(L) for insert, search, and startsWith, where L is the length of the input word or prefix.
implement-trie-prefix-tree.space: O(N * L * Sigma) total memory in worst case with no shared prefixes, where Sigma is the alphabet size (26) and N is the total number of words inserted.

implement-stack-using-queues.title: Implement Stack using Queues
implement-stack-using-queues.insight: A queue gives us FIFO order, but a stack needs LIFO. If we append a new element to the back of a queue of size k, it is at the very tail. If we immediately dequeue the k preceding elements one by one and re-enqueue them at the back, the new item naturally lands at the front of the queue. That means front is top, so pop and top become effortless O(1) operations.
implement-stack-using-queues.approach:
1. Initialise a single FIFO queue `q` in the constructor.
2. For `push(x)`: record the current size `sz = len(q)`.
3. Enqueue `x` to the back of `q`.
4. Loop `sz` times: dequeue the front element and immediately enqueue it back to the tail.
5. For `pop()`: simply dequeue and return the front element of `q` (which is now O(1)).
6. For `top()`: inspect and return the front element of `q` without removing it (O(1)).
7. For `empty()`: return whether `q` has a length of 0 (O(1)).
implement-stack-using-queues.time: O(n) for push, O(1) for pop, top, and empty.
implement-stack-using-queues.space: O(n) total auxiliary space to hold the n elements in a single queue.

capacity-to-ship-packages-within-d-days.title: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days
capacity-to-ship-packages-within-d-days.insight: The problem exhibits monotonicity: if capacity C is sufficient to ship everything within D days, any capacity greater than C is also sufficient. Because the predicate is monotonic (False, False, ..., True, True), we can binary search the capacity in the range [max(weights), sum(weights)], testing feasibility in O(N) time with a greedy pass.
capacity-to-ship-packages-within-d-days.approach:
Set the search range: `low = max(weights)` (since the ship must hold the heaviest package) and `high = sum(weights)` (shipping everything in 1 day).
Run a binary search loop while `low < high`.
Calculate candidate capacity `mid = low + (high - low) // 2`.
Simulate the shipping process using a helper function `canShip(cap)`.
Inside the helper, maintain `days_needed = 1` and `current_load = 0`.
Iterate through each weight: if `current_load + w > cap`, start a new day by setting `days_needed += 1` and `current_load = w`; otherwise add `w` to `current_load`.
If `canShip(mid)` returns true (`days_needed <= days`), `mid` might be our answer or too big, so shrink the upper bound: `high = mid`.
If false, `mid` is too small, so increase the lower bound: `low = mid + 1`.
When `low == high`, return `low`.

minimum-add-to-make-parentheses-valid.title: Minimum Add to Make Parentheses Valid
minimum-add-to-make-parentheses-valid.insight: Every ')' must match with the nearest available preceding '('. If we see a ')' and our balance of open brackets is zero, that ')' can never be matched by any future '(' — it demands an immediate insertion before it. Any '(' left over at the end can never be closed by the input string, so each one requires an appended ')' at the end.
minimum-add-to-make-parentheses-valid.approach:
Initialise two integer counters: `open_needed` set to 0 (for unmatched '(') and `close_needed` set to 0 (for unmatched ')').
Iterate through each character `char` in the string `s`.
If `char` is '(', increment `open_needed` by 1.
If `char` is ')', check if `open_needed > 0`.
If `open_needed > 0`, we have a valid open bracket to pair with, so decrement `open_needed` by 1.
Otherwise, this ')' has no preceding '(', so increment `close_needed` by 1.
After the loop finishes, return the sum of `open_needed` and `close_needed`.

convert-sorted-list-to-binary-search-tre.title: Convert Sorted List to Binary Search Tree
convert-sorted-list-to-binary-search-tre.insight: An inorder traversal of a BST processes values in strictly ascending sorted order, which is the exact order of our linked list. If we know the total size N, we can simulate the inorder build: recursively construct the left subtree of size N/2, assign the current list node's value to the root, advance our linked list pointer by one step, and then recursively construct the right subtree. This achieves O(N) time with only O(log N) recursion stack space.
convert-sorted-list-to-binary-search-tre.approach:
Traverse the linked list once to count the total number of nodes, N.
Keep a pointer `curr` referencing the head of the linked list that persists across recursive calls.
Define a helper function `build(left, right)` to construct a balanced BST from index range `[left, right]` inclusive.
Base case: if `left > right`, return `None` (empty subtree).
Calculate the midpoint: `mid = (left + right) // 2`.
Recurse on the left half: `left_child = build(left, mid - 1)`.
Create the root node `TreeNode(curr.val)`, link `root.left = left_child`, and advance `curr = curr.next`.
Recurse on the right half: `root.right = build(mid + 1, right)`.
Return `root` from the helper and invoke `build(0, N - 1)`.
convert-sorted-list-to-binary-search-tre.solution:
# Definition for singly-linked list.
# class ListNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.next = next
# Definition for a binary tree node.
# class TreeNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.left = left
#         self.right = right

class Solution:
    def sortedListToBST(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[TreeNode]:
        # 1. Count list length
        size = 0
        curr = head
        while curr:
            size += 1
            curr = curr.next
        
        self.curr = head
        
        # 2. Inorder tree construction
        def build(left: int, right: int) -> Optional[TreeNode]:
            if left > right:
                return None
            
            mid = (left + right) // 2
            
            # Build left subtree
            left_child = build(left, mid - 1)
            
            # Process current root
            root = TreeNode(self.curr.val)
            root.left = left_child
            self.curr = self.curr.next
            
            # Build right subtree
            root.right = build(mid + 1, right)
            
            return root
        
        return build(0, size - 1)

summary-ranges.title: Summary Ranges
summary-ranges.insight: Since `nums` is strictly sorted, every consecutive range satisfies `nums[j] == nums[i] + (j - i)`. We just need a single pass with two pointers: keep `start` pinned to the beginning of the current range, extend `end` as far as elements increase by exactly 1, then append the formatted string.
summary-ranges.approach:
1. Check if `nums` is empty; if so, immediately return an empty list.
2. Initialise an empty results list `res` and an index `i = 0`.
3. Enter a while loop that runs while `i < len(nums)`.
4. Store the start value `start = nums[i]`.
5. Use an inner while loop to advance `i` as long as `i + 1 < len(nums)` and `nums[i + 1] == nums[i] + 1`.
6. Check if `start == nums[i]`: if true, append `str(start)` to `res`.
7. Otherwise, append `f'{start}->{nums[i]}'` to `res`.
8. Increment `i` by 1 to move to the start of the next potential range.
9. Return `res`.

invert-binary-tree.title: Invert Binary Tree
invert-binary-tree.insight: A tree is an inverted version of itself if and only if its left and right subtrees are inverted and swapped. Because of this self-similarity, swapping `root.left` and `root.right` at every node via standard post-order or pre-order traversal completely mirrors the tree.
invert-binary-tree.approach:
Check the base case: if `root` is null, simply return null.
Recursively call the inversion function on `root.left` and hold the result.
Recursively call the inversion function on `root.right` and hold the result.
Assign the inverted right subtree to `root.left`.
Assign the inverted left subtree to `root.right`.
Return `root` to allow callers higher up the call stack to link correctly.
invert-binary-tree.solution:
# Definition for a binary tree node.
# class TreeNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.left = left
#         self.right = right
class Solution:
    def invertTree(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> Optional[TreeNode]:
        if not root:
            return None
        
        # Invert both subtrees first
        left_inverted = self.invertTree(root.left)
        right_inverted = self.invertTree(root.right)
        
        # Swap them on the current node
        root.left, root.right = right_inverted, left_inverted
        
        return root

odd-even-linked-list.title: Odd Even Linked List
odd-even-linked-list.insight: Because odd and even nodes alternate perfectly, `odd.next` is always `even.next`, and the subsequent `even.next` is `odd.next.next`. We can rewire both chains concurrently in a single pass while caching `evenHead`, connecting `odd.next = evenHead` once `even` reaches the end.
odd-even-linked-list.approach:
1. Handle edge cases: if `head` is None or `head.next` is None, return `head` immediately.
2. Initialise `odd = head`, `even = head.next`, and save `even_head = even` so we can attach it later.
3. Loop while `even` and `even.next` are both non-null.
4. Point `odd.next` to `even.next` and advance `odd = odd.next`.
5. Point `even.next` to `odd.next` and advance `even = even.next`.
6. After the loop, connect the end of the odd chain to the saved `even_head` via `odd.next = even_head`.
7. Return `head`.
odd-even-linked-list.solution:
# Definition for singly-linked list.
# class ListNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.next = next

class Solution:
    def oddEvenList(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        if not head or not head.next:
            return head
        
        odd = head
        even = head.next
        even_head = even
        
        # even is ahead, so checking even and even.next covers odd bounds
        while even and even.next:
            odd.next = even.next
            odd = odd.next
            even.next = odd.next
            even = even.next
            
        # Stitch odd tail to even head
        odd.next = even_head
        return head

word-ladder-ii.title: Word Ladder II
word-ladder-ii.insight: Instead of duplicating paths in the BFS queue, separate the search into two phases: first, run BFS level-by-level just to find the shortest distance from beginWord to each word and record parent-to-child edges in a DAG. We only remove words from the candidate pool at the end of each BFS level, allowing multiple parents from the same level to link to the same child. Second, run a simple DFS backtrack from beginWord to endWord along those recorded DAG edges to assemble all paths without any wasted exploration.
word-ladder-ii.approach:
1. Convert wordList to a hash set for O(1) lookups; return [] immediately if endWord is not in the set.
2. Initialise current level set as {beginWord}, parent-to-children mapping adj = defaultdict(list), and a flag found = False.
3. While the current level is non-empty and endWord hasn't been found, remove current level words from the word set so we don't visit them in subsequent deeper levels.
4. For each word in the current level, generate all 1-character mutations. If a mutation exists in the remaining word set, record it in next_level and append to adj[word].
5. If endWord is generated in this level, set found = True.
6. Update current level to next_level; break after the level finishes if found is True.
7. If found is False, return [].
8. Perform a DFS backtrack starting at beginWord using adj to collect all complete paths ending at endWord.
9. Return the collected list of paths.

largest-divisible-subset.title: Largest Divisible Subset
largest-divisible-subset.insight: Divisibility is transitive: if a divides b and b divides c, then a divides c. By sorting the array in ascending order, if a new number nums[i] is divisible by the largest element in an existing valid subset nums[j], it is guaranteed to be divisible by every element in that subset. This reduces the problem directly to finding the Longest Increasing Subsequence with divisibility as the condition.
largest-divisible-subset.approach:
1. Sort nums in ascending order so we only ever need to check divisibility against the largest existing element in a chain.
2. Initialise a DP array `dp` of size N with 1s, where `dp[i]` represents the length of the largest divisible subset ending at `nums[i]`.
3. Initialise a `parent` array of size N with -1 to store the index of the previous element in the optimal chain.
4. Track `max_len = 1` and `max_idx = 0` to know where the longest chain ends.
5. Loop `i` from 1 to N - 1, and inner loop `j` from 0 to i - 1.
6. If `nums[i] % nums[j] == 0` and `dp[j] + 1 > dp[i]`, update `dp[i] = dp[j] + 1` and `parent[i] = j`.
7. If `dp[i] > max_len`, update `max_len = dp[i]` and `max_idx = i`.
8. Reconstruct the subset by following `parent` pointers backwards starting from `max_idx` until hitting -1, then return the collected elements.

delete-nodes-and-return-forest.title: Delete Nodes And Return Forest
delete-nodes-and-return-forest.insight: A node is a root of a new tree if and only if two conditions hold: it is not deleted, and either it was the original root or its direct parent was deleted. Passing an `is_root` flag down during DFS makes root identification effortless.
delete-nodes-and-return-forest.approach:
Convert `to_delete` into a hash set `to_delete_set` for O(1) lookups.
Initialise an empty list `forest` to store the roots of the resulting trees.
Define a helper `dfs(node, is_root)` that returns the (possibly updated or null) subtree reference.
Base case: if `node` is `None`, return `None` immediately.
Check if the current node needs deleting: `deleted = node.val in to_delete_set`.
If `is_root` is true and `not deleted`, append `node` to `forest`.
Recurse on left and right children, passing `is_root = deleted` so children know if their parent was removed.
Update `node.left` and `node.right` with the return values of those recursive calls to sever links to deleted children.
Return `None` if `deleted` is true, otherwise return `node`.
Invoke `dfs(root, is_root=True)` and return `forest`.

customer-who-visited-but-did-not-make-an.title: Customer Who Visited but Did Not Make Any Transactions
customer-who-visited-but-did-not-make-an.insight: This is a textbook anti-join problem. We want records in Visits that have no corresponding record in Transactions. A LEFT JOIN followed by `WHERE t.transaction_id IS NULL` isolates those exact visits, and a simple `GROUP BY customer_id` with `COUNT(*)` gives us the answer in a single pass.
customer-who-visited-but-did-not-make-an.approach:
1. Start with the Visits table aliased as v.
2. Perform a LEFT JOIN with Transactions aliased as t on v.visit_id = t.visit_id.
3. Add a WHERE condition `t.transaction_id IS NULL` to discard visits that had transactions.
4. Group the filtered rows by `v.customer_id`.
5. Select `v.customer_id` alongside `COUNT(*) AS count_no_trans`.
6. Return the resulting aggregated table.
customer-who-visited-but-did-not-make-an.solution:
import pandas as pd

def find_customers(visits: pd.DataFrame, transactions: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    # Left merge visits with transactions
    merged = visits.merge(transactions, on='visit_id', how='left')
    
    # Keep visits with no transactions (anti-join)
    no_trans = merged[merged['transaction_id'].isna()]
    
    # Group by customer and count visits
    res = no_trans.groupby('customer_id', as_index=False).agg(
        count_no_trans=('visit_id', 'count')
    )
    return res

minimum-falling-path-sum.title: Minimum Falling Path Sum
minimum-falling-path-sum.insight: The minimum sum to reach cell (r, c) depends strictly on the minimum sums to reach (r-1, c-1), (r-1, c), and (r-1, c+1). Since calculating row r only ever requires values from row r-1, we can compute row by row downwards and compress our DP storage to just a single previous-row array of size n.
minimum-falling-path-sum.approach:
Check if n == 1; if so, return matrix[0][0] straight away.
Initialise a 1D array `prev` as a copy of the first row `matrix[0]`.
Iterate through rows `r` from 1 up to `n - 1`.
Initialise a fresh array `curr` of length `n` for the current row.
For each column `c` from 0 to `n - 1`, identify valid predecessors from `prev`: `prev[c]`, and conditionally `prev[c - 1]` (if c > 0) and `prev[c + 1]` (if c < n - 1).
Set `curr[c] = matrix[r][c] + min(valid predecessors)`.
Set `prev = curr` before advancing to the next row.
Return the minimum value in `prev` after processing all rows.

h-index.title: H-Index
h-index.insight: A researcher with n papers can never have an h-index greater than n. This means any paper with citations greater than n can simply be capped and treated as having n citations. We can create an array of n + 1 buckets where bucket[i] stores how many papers have exactly i citations (with bucket[n] holding all papers with n or more), and then scan backwards accumulating counts.
h-index.approach:
1. Let n be the length of the citations array.
2. Allocate a buckets array of size n + 1 initialised to zeros.
3. Iterate through citations: if citations[i] >= n, increment buckets[n], else increment buckets[citations[i]].
4. Initialise a running sum total = 0 to track the number of papers seen so far from highest citations downwards.
5. Loop i from n down to 0.
6. Add buckets[i] to total.
7. The first time total >= i, return i as the maximum valid h-index.
8. If the loop completes without returning, return 0.

find-the-length-of-the-longest-common-pr.title: Find the Length of the Longest Common Prefix
find-the-length-of-the-longest-common-pr.insight: Because numbers are at most 10^8, each integer has at most 8-9 prefixes (generated cheaply by repeatedly dividing by 10). Storing all prefixes from arr1 produces at most 400,000 integers in a hash set, turning arr2 lookups into constant-time prefix checks.
find-the-length-of-the-longest-common-pr.approach:
Initialise an empty hash set called `prefixes` to store all integer prefixes from `arr1`.
Iterate through each number `x` in `arr1`.
Repeatedly insert `x` into `prefixes` and update `x = x // 10` until `x == 0`.
Initialise `max_len = 0` to record the length of the longest common prefix found.
Iterate through each number `y` in `arr2`.
While `y > 0`, check if `y` is present in `prefixes`.
If `y` is in `prefixes`, update `max_len = max(max_len, len(str(y)))` and break early for this `y` since smaller prefixes of `y` cannot yield a larger length.
If `y` is not in `prefixes`, strip its last digit via `y = y // 10` and continue checking.
Return `max_len` after checking all elements in `arr2`.

find-numbers-with-even-number-of-digits.title: Find Numbers with Even Number of Digits
find-numbers-with-even-number-of-digits.insight: The number of digits in a positive integer `n` can be found either by counting how many times we can divide by 10 until it hits 0, or directly via `floor(log10(n)) + 1`. Since numbers are capped at 10^5, an even digit count simply means having 2, 4, or 6 digits.
find-numbers-with-even-number-of-digits.approach:
1. Initialise a counter `even_digit_count = 0` to track valid numbers.
2. Loop through each number `num` in `nums`.
3. Implement a helper or inline loop to count the digits of `num`.
4. Set `digits = 0` and while `num > 0`, do `num //= 10` and increment `digits`.
5. Check if `digits % 2 == 0`.
6. If true, increment `even_digit_count`.
7. After examining all numbers, return `even_digit_count`.

simplify-path.title: Simplify Path
simplify-path.insight: Splitting the string on '/' automatically handles multiple consecutive slashes by producing empty strings. Because directory navigation has Last-In-First-Out behaviour when going up a directory, a stack allows us to process tokens in a single linear pass.
simplify-path.approach:
Split the input string 'path' using '/' as the delimiter to obtain a list of components.
Initialise an empty list 'stack' to hold valid directory names.
Iterate through each component in the split list.
If the component is empty '' or '.', ignore it as it represents redundant slashes or current directory.
If the component is '..', pop the top element from 'stack' if the stack is non-empty.
Otherwise, the component is a valid directory name (including '...' etc.), so push it onto 'stack'.
Join the elements in 'stack' with '/' and prepend a leading '/' to form the canonical path.
Return the joined string.

palindrome-partitioning-ii.title: Palindrome Partitioning II
palindrome-partitioning-ii.insight: Instead of precomputing an O(N^2) 2D boolean palindrome table, we can merge palindrome discovery with DP. For each centre (both odd and even), expand outward while characters match; whenever s[l..r] is a palindrome, dp[r] is at most dp[l-1] + 1 (or 0 if l == 0), taking O(N) auxiliary space.
palindrome-partitioning-ii.approach:
1. Let n = len(s). Initialize an array dp of size n where dp[i] = i (the worst case: i cuts for prefix s[0..i]).
2. Iterate through each index i from 0 to n - 1 treating it as a palindrome centre.
3. Handle odd-length palindromes by setting l = i, r = i.
4. Whilst l >= 0 and r < n and s[l] == s[r], update dp[r]: if l == 0 then dp[r] = 0, else dp[r] = min(dp[r], dp[l-1] + 1). Decrement l, increment r.
5. Handle even-length palindromes by setting l = i, r = i + 1.
6. Whilst l >= 0 and r < n and s[l] == s[r], update dp[r] using the exact same rule, then decrement l, increment r.
7. After visiting all centres, return dp[n-1].
palindrome-partitioning-ii.solution:
class Solution:
    def minCut(self, s: str) -> int:
        n = len(s)
        # dp[i] stores min cuts for prefix s[0..i]
        # Base case: cutting every character requires i cuts
        dp = list(range(n))
        
        for mid in range(n):
            # Odd-length palindromes centered at mid
            l, r = mid, mid
            while l >= 0 and r < n and s[l] == s[r]:
                dp[r] = 0 if l == 0 else min(dp[r], dp[l - 1] + 1)
                l -= 1
                r += 1
                
            # Even-length palindromes centered between mid and mid + 1
            l, r = mid, mid + 1
            while l >= 0 and r < n and s[l] == s[r]:
                dp[r] = 0 if l == 0 else min(dp[r], dp[l - 1] + 1)
                l -= 1
                r += 1
                
        return dp[-1]

search-in-rotated-sorted-array-ii.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array II
search-in-rotated-sorted-array-ii.insight: In standard rotated binary search, comparing nums[mid] with nums[left] tells us definitively which half is sorted. With duplicates, if nums[left] == nums[mid] == nums[right], we cannot deduce which half contains the pivot (e.g. [1, 0, 1, 1, 1] vs [1, 1, 1, 0, 1]), so we simply contract the search window with left += 1 and right -= 1 until the ambiguity clears.
search-in-rotated-sorted-array-ii.approach:
1. Initialise left = 0 and right = len(nums) - 1.
2. Loop whilst left <= right.
3. Compute mid = left + (right - left) // 2.
4. If nums[mid] == target, return True immediately.
5. If nums[left] == nums[mid] == nums[right], increment left by 1 and decrement right by 1, then continue.
6. If the left half is sorted (nums[left] <= nums[mid]): check if target falls in [nums[left], nums[mid]); if yes, right = mid - 1, else left = mid + 1.
7. Else (right half is sorted): check if target falls in (nums[mid], nums[right]]; if yes, left = mid + 1, else right = mid - 1.
8. If the loop exits without a match, return False.

game-play-analysis-i.title: Game Play Analysis I
game-play-analysis-i.insight: Since we need the earliest record per distinct entity, this maps directly to a `MIN(event_date)` aggregation grouped by `player_id`. If we need other row attributes later, window functions like `ROW_NUMBER()` would be the way, but for just the minimum date, simple aggregation is optimal and cleanest.
game-play-analysis-i.approach:
Identify the grouping key: we need one row per `player_id`.
Identify the target aggregate: we want the earliest date, which is `MIN(event_date)`.
Alias the resulting aggregate column as `first_login` to match the required schema.
Apply `GROUP BY player_id` on the `Activity` table.
Verify no filtering (WHERE clause) is needed since all rows represent valid logins.
game-play-analysis-i.solution:
import pandas as pd

def game_analysis(activity: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    # Group by player_id and calculate minimum event_date
    df = activity.groupby('player_id')['event_date'].min().reset_index()
    # Rename event_date to first_login
    df.rename(columns={'event_date': 'first_login'}, inplace=True)
    return df

add-strings.title: Add Strings
add-strings.insight: We align the numbers by their least significant digits and move backwards. At each step, the total sum is `digit1 + digit2 + carry`. We write `sum % 10` to our result and pass `sum // 10` to the next column, continuing whilst either string has digits left or the carry is non-zero.
add-strings.approach:
1. Initialise pointer `i = len(num1) - 1`, pointer `j = len(num2) - 1`, and integer `carry = 0`.
2. Initialise an empty list (or StringBuilder) `res` to collect the result digits in reverse.
3. Loop while `i >= 0`, `j >= 0`, or `carry > 0`.
4. Set `total = carry` at the start of each iteration.
5. If `i >= 0`, extract digit `ord(num1[i]) - ord('0')`, add it to `total`, and decrement `i`.
6. If `j >= 0`, extract digit `ord(num2[j]) - ord('0')`, add it to `total`, and decrement `j`.
7. Append `str(total % 10)` to `res` and update `carry = total // 10`.
8. Once the loop ends, reverse `res` and join it into a single string to return.

maximum-sum-circular-subarray.title: Maximum Sum Circular Subarray
maximum-sum-circular-subarray.insight: A circular subarray either doesn't wrap around at all, or it wraps across the boundary. If it wraps around, the elements we leave out form a contiguous *minimum* subarray in the middle. Hence, the circular max sum is simply `total_sum - min_subarray_sum`. The only catch is if all numbers are negative, `total_sum == min_subarray_sum`, which would leave us with an invalid empty subarray (sum 0) — in that case, we simply return the normal Kadane's maximum.
maximum-sum-circular-subarray.approach:
1. Maintain variables for `total_sum`, `cur_max`, `max_sum`, `cur_min`, and `min_sum`, initialising max/min trackers with the first element.
2. Iterate through each number in the array in a single pass.
3. Add the current number to `total_sum`.
4. Update `cur_max` using standard Kadane: `max(x, cur_max + x)` and update `max_sum`.
5. Update `cur_min` using inverted Kadane: `min(x, cur_min + x)` and update `min_sum`.
6. After the loop, check if `max_sum < 0` (meaning every element in the array is negative).
7. If all negative, return `max_sum` directly to prevent returning an empty subarray sum of 0.
8. Otherwise, return `max(max_sum, total_sum - min_sum)`.
maximum-sum-circular-subarray.solution:
class Solution:
    def maxSubarraySumCircular(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        total_sum = 0
        cur_max = 0
        max_sum = nums[0]
        cur_min = 0
        min_sum = nums[0]
        
        for x in nums:
            # Kadane's for maximum subarray
            cur_max = max(x, cur_max + x)
            max_sum = max(max_sum, cur_max)
            
            # Kadane's for minimum subarray
            cur_min = min(x, cur_min + x)
            min_sum = min(min_sum, cur_min)
            
            total_sum += x
        
        # If all numbers are negative, max_sum is the largest single element
        # and total_sum - min_sum would incorrectly yield 0 (empty subarray)
        if max_sum < 0:
            return max_sum
            
        return max(max_sum, total_sum - min_sum)

delete-the-middle-node-of-a-linked-list.title: Delete the Middle Node of a Linked List
delete-the-middle-node-of-a-linked-list.insight: By introducing a dummy node pointing to the head and starting slow at the dummy while fast starts at head, slow stays one step behind the standard middle finder. When fast reaches the end by taking two steps at a time, slow lands cleanly on the node right before the middle, making the deletion a simple one-line pointer skip without extra tracking.
delete-the-middle-node-of-a-linked-list.approach:
1. Check if head is null or head.next is null; if there's only one node, return null immediately.
2. Initialise a dummy node whose next pointer references head.
3. Set slow pointing to dummy and fast pointing to head.
4. Loop while fast is not null and fast.next is not null.
5. Advance slow by one node (slow = slow.next).
6. Advance fast by two nodes (fast = fast.next.next).
7. Once the loop terminates, slow is guaranteed to point to the node immediately before the middle node.
8. Re-link slow.next to slow.next.next to drop the middle node.
9. Return dummy.next, which is the head of the updated list.
delete-the-middle-node-of-a-linked-list.solution:
# Definition for singly-linked list.
# class ListNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.next = next
class Solution:
    def deleteMiddle(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        # If single node, deleting middle leaves an empty list
        if not head or not head.next:
            return None
        
        # Dummy node ensures slow stays one step behind the middle
        dummy = ListNode(0, head)
        slow = dummy
        fast = head
        
        while fast and fast.next:
            slow = slow.next
            fast = fast.next.next
            
        # slow is now at predecessor of middle node; bypass middle
        slow.next = slow.next.next
        
        return dummy.next

minimum-number-of-arrows-to-burst-balloo.title: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons
minimum-number-of-arrows-to-burst-balloo.insight: Every balloon must be popped, including the one that ends earliest. To give that required arrow the best possible chance of popping other balloons as well, our best greedy choice is to shoot it at that balloon's right boundary (x_end). Any balloon starting after this position cannot be burst by this arrow and will require a fresh one.
minimum-number-of-arrows-to-burst-balloo.approach:
Sort the balloons in ascending order of their end coordinate (points[i][1]).
Initialise arrow count to 1 because at least one arrow is required for the first balloon.
Set the current arrow's position (last_arrow) to the end coordinate of the first balloon (points[0][1]).
Iterate through the remaining balloons starting from index 1.
For each balloon [start, end], compare start with last_arrow.
If start > last_arrow, the balloon starts strictly after the current arrow, so it cannot be burst by it.
In that case, increment arrow count by 1 and move last_arrow to this balloon's end.
If start <= last_arrow, this balloon already covers the arrow position, so it's burst for free; do nothing.
Return the total arrow count.

subarrays-distinct-element-sum-of-square.title: Subarrays Distinct Element Sum of Squares I
subarrays-distinct-element-sum-of-square.insight: Instead of recomputing the set from scratch for every subarray, fix the start index i and expand j to the right. Inserting nums[j] into an existing set takes O(1) time on average, allowing us to update the distinct count incrementally and achieve O(n^2) overall time.
subarrays-distinct-element-sum-of-square.approach:
1. Initialise total_sum to 0.
2. Determine n, the length of nums.
3. Loop with outer pointer i from 0 to n - 1 to represent the start of the subarray.
4. Inside the outer loop, initialise an empty hash set seen.
5. Loop with inner pointer j from i to n - 1 to represent the end of the subarray.
6. Add nums[j] to seen.
7. Take the current size of seen (len(seen)), square it, and add it to total_sum.
8. After both loops terminate, return total_sum.

monthly-transactions-i.title: Monthly Transactions I
monthly-transactions-i.insight: Instead of splitting the data and joining back, we do conditional aggregation in a single scan. In SQL, `SUM(CASE WHEN state = 'approved' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` allows us to calculate both approved metrics in the same `GROUP BY` statement as total metrics.
monthly-transactions-i.approach:
1. Truncate or format `trans_date` to the first 7 characters (`YYYY-MM`).
2. Group the rows by `month` and `country` (ensuring NULL countries are preserved in the group).
3. Count total transactions using `COUNT(id)` or `COUNT(*)`.
4. Compute `approved_count` by summing 1 when `state = 'approved'` and 0 otherwise.
5. Compute `trans_total_amount` using `SUM(amount)`.
6. Compute `approved_total_amount` by summing `amount` when `state = 'approved'` and 0 otherwise.
7. Return the resulting aggregated columns.
monthly-transactions-i.solution:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

def monthly_transactions(transactions: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    # Return empty table structure if input has no rows
    if transactions.empty:
        return pd.DataFrame(columns=[
            'month', 'country', 'trans_count', 
            'approved_count', 'trans_total_amount', 'approved_total_amount'
        ])
    
    # Extract 'YYYY-MM' from trans_date
    transactions['month'] = transactions['trans_date'].astype(str).str[:7]
    
    # Indicator and amount columns for approved transactions
    is_approved = transactions['state'] == 'approved'
    transactions['is_approved'] = is_approved.astype(int)
    transactions['approved_amount'] = np.where(is_approved, transactions['amount'], 0)
    
    # Group by month and country with conditional aggregates
    res = transactions.groupby(['month', 'country'], dropna=False).agg(
        trans_count=('id', 'count'),
        approved_count=('is_approved', 'sum'),
        trans_total_amount=('amount', 'sum'),
        approved_total_amount=('approved_amount', 'sum')
    ).reset_index()
    
    return res

max-area-of-island.title: Max Area of Island
max-area-of-island.insight: Each land cell belongs to exactly one connected component. Sinking visited land (overwriting 1 with 0) immediately upon visiting prevents re-processing and eliminates the need for an external visited set, keeping the traversal lean and strictly linear.
max-area-of-island.approach:
1. Read grid dimensions `rows` and `cols`, and initialise `max_area = 0`.
2. Define a recursive helper `dfs(r, c)` that returns the area of the island reachable from `(r, c)`.
3. In `dfs`, return 0 immediately if `(r, c)` is out of bounds or `grid[r][c] == 0`.
4. Sink the current cell by setting `grid[r][c] = 0` to mark it as visited.
5. Return `1` plus the recursive calls to all four neighbours: up, down, left, right.
6. Iterate with nested loops through every cell `(r, c)` in the grid.
7. If `grid[r][c] == 1`, call `dfs(r, c)` and update `max_area = max(max_area, area)`.
8. Return `max_area` after scanning all cells.

movie-rating.title: Movie Rating
movie-rating.insight: The problem asks for two completely orthogonal aggregations stacked into one column; in SQL this is classic `(SELECT ...) UNION ALL (SELECT ...)`. In Python/Pandas, compute the top user by rating count (descending) and name (ascending), compute top movie in Feb 2020 by mean rating (descending) and title (ascending), then combine into a 2-row DataFrame.
movie-rating.approach:
Filter `movie_rating` for dates starting with '2020-02' (or between '2020-02-01' and '2020-02-29').
Merge ratings with `users` to associate user names with their review counts.
Group by user name, count distinct reviews, sort by count descending, then user name ascending.
Pick the top-1 user name from this sorted group.
Merge the February ratings subset with `movies` to associate titles with ratings.
Group by movie title, calculate mean rating, sort by mean rating descending, then title ascending.
Pick the top-1 movie title from this sorted group.
Construct and return a DataFrame with column name `results` containing `[top_user, top_movie]`.
movie-rating.time: O(R + U log U + M log M) where R is rows in MovieRating, U is unique users, and M is unique movies.
movie-rating.space: O(R + U + M) to store merged intermediate DataFrames and aggregation tables.
movie-rating.solution:
import pandas as pd

def movie_rating(movies: pd.DataFrame, users: pd.DataFrame, movie_rating: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    # 1. Find user with the greatest number of ratings (tie-break: name ASC)
    user_counts = (
        movie_rating.merge(users, on='user_id')
        .groupby('name')
        .size()
        .reset_index(name='count')
        .sort_values(by=['count', 'name'], ascending=[False, True])
    )
    top_user = user_counts.iloc[0]['name']

    # 2. Find movie with highest average rating in Feb 2020 (tie-break: title ASC)
    feb_ratings = movie_rating[
        movie_rating['created_at'].astype(str).str.startswith('2020-02')
    ]
    movie_avgs = (
        feb_ratings.merge(movies, on='movie_id')
        .groupby('title')['rating']
        .mean()
        .reset_index(name='avg_rating')
        .sort_values(by=['avg_rating', 'title'], ascending=[False, True])
    )
    top_movie = movie_avgs.iloc[0]['title']

    # 3. Stack results into single column
    return pd.DataFrame({'results': [top_user, top_movie]})

count-salary-categories.title: Count Salary Categories
count-salary-categories.insight: Because SQL's GROUP BY only outputs groups present in the data, categories with zero records disappear. The cleanest way around this is either three separate SELECT queries glued together with UNION ALL, or a static table of categories LEFT JOINed to the aggregated data with IFNULL/COALESCE.
count-salary-categories.approach:
Identify the three disjoint income conditions: income < 20000, income BETWEEN 20000 AND 50000, and income > 50000.
Draft a standalone query for 'Low Salary' selecting the literal category name and SUM(income < 20000) or COUNT(1) with WHERE income < 20000.
Draft an identical query structure for 'Average Salary' filtering for income BETWEEN 20000 AND 50000.
Draft an identical query structure for 'High Salary' filtering for income > 50000.
Combine all three subqueries using UNION ALL so no duplicate filtering occurs.
In Python / Pandas, construct a DataFrame with the three fixed category names and compute counts by boolean indexing on the income column.
count-salary-categories.solution:
import pandas as pd

def count_salary_categories(accounts: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    # Calculate counts using boolean filtering directly
    low_count = int((accounts['income'] < 20000).sum())
    avg_count = int(((accounts['income'] >= 20000) & (accounts['income'] <= 50000)).sum())
    high_count = int((accounts['income'] > 50000).sum())
    
    # Always return all three categories even if zero
    return pd.DataFrame({
        'category': ['Low Salary', 'Average Salary', 'High Salary'],
        'accounts_count': [low_count, avg_count, high_count]
    })

count-subarrays-with-majority-element-i.title: Count Subarrays With Majority Element I
count-subarrays-with-majority-element-i.insight: Transform every element equal to target into +1 and every other element into -1.
