A subarray has target as majority if and only if its sum in the transformed array is strictly positive, meaning prefix[j] - prefix[i] > 0 (or prefix[j] > prefix[i] for j > i). This turns the problem into counting pairs (i, j) where i < j and prefix[i] < prefix[j], solvable in O(N log N) using a Fenwick Tree with offset indexing or Merge Sort.
count-subarrays-with-majority-element-i.approach:
Initialize total answer to 0 and current prefix sum to 0.
The prefix sum ranges from -N to +N, so use an offset of N + 1 to keep all Fenwick Tree indices positive (1 to 2N + 1).
Create a Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree) of size 2N + 2 to support point updates and prefix query operations.
Insert the initial prefix sum 0 into the Fenwick Tree before scanning (offset value N + 1).
Iterate through each element x in nums.
Add +1 to current prefix sum if x == target, else subtract 1.
Query the Fenwick Tree for the count of previously seen prefix sums strictly less than current prefix sum.
Add that count to the answer.
Update the Fenwick tree by adding 1 at the current prefix sum's shifted index.
Return the total answer.

number-of-zigzag-arrays-ii.title: Number of ZigZag Arrays II
number-of-zigzag-arrays-ii.insight: Notice that the transitions between length k and length k+1 are strictly linear and identical across all steps. Since m <= 75, our state space has only 2m <= 150 states (value in [0, m-1] plus whether the last move was UP or DOWN). This means we can express the transition as a constant (2m x 2m) adjacency matrix and raise it to the power (n - 2) using binary exponentiation in O(m^3 log n) time.
number-of-zigzag-arrays-ii.approach:
Let m = r - l + 1. The problem only depends on m, not the absolute values of l and r.
Define a state vector of size 2m: the first m entries represent ending at value x after an UP move, and the next m entries represent ending at value x after a DOWN move.
Construct the initial vector V for length 2: V[x] = x for UP states (0 <= x < m) and V[m + x] = m - 1 - x for DOWN states.
Construct a (2m x 2m) transition matrix T: from state UP(x), add an edge to DOWN(y) for all y < x; from state DOWN(x), add an edge to UP(y) for all y > x.
Implement binary matrix exponentiation to compute T^(n - 2) % MOD in O((2m)^3 log n) steps.
Multiply the initial vector V by the resulting matrix T^(n - 2).
Sum all elements in the resulting vector modulo 10^9 + 7 and return.

customers-who-never-order.title: Customers Who Never Order
customers-who-never-order.insight: This is a classic anti-join. We want elements in set A that have no counterpart in set B. In SQL, a `LEFT JOIN` preserves all rows from Customers and populates missing Orders columns with NULL; filtering `WHERE Orders.id IS NULL` isolates customers with zero orders. In application code (Pandas or Java), loading order customer IDs into a hash set gives O(1) membership checks, reducing the entire operation to a single linear pass.
customers-who-never-order.approach:
Extract all distinct customer IDs present in the Orders table into a lookup set.
Perform a left outer join between Customers and Orders on Customers.id == Orders.customerId (or filter Customers directly).
Identify rows where the order record failed to match (i.e. order id is NaN/null).
Select the customer name column from these unmatched rows.
Rename the column to 'Customers' to match the schema contract.
Return the resulting dataframe/list.
customers-who-never-order.solution:
import pandas as pd

def find_customers(customers: pd.DataFrame, orders: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    # Identify customer IDs that appear in the orders table
    ordered_ids = set(orders['customerId'])
    
    # Filter customers whose id is not present in ordered_ids
    no_orders = customers[~customers['id'].isin(ordered_ids)]
    
    # Select and rename the 'name' column as required
    return no_orders[['name']].rename(columns={'name': 'Customers'})

# Equivalent SQL:
# SELECT c.name AS Customers
# FROM Customers c
# LEFT JOIN Orders o ON c.id = o.customerId
# WHERE o.id IS NULL;

remove-outermost-parentheses.title: Remove Outermost Parentheses
remove-outermost-parentheses.insight: We don't need to slice or store primitive segments. An opening bracket '(' is an outer bracket if and only if our depth before seeing it is 0. A closing bracket ')' is an outer bracket if and only if our depth after seeing it is 0. Everything else is internal structure and gets preserved.
remove-outermost-parentheses.approach:
Initialise an empty list `res` to collect internal characters.
Initialise an integer `depth = 0` to track the nesting level.
Loop through each character `ch` in string `s`.
If `ch == '('`: check if `depth > 0`. If true, append `ch` to `res`. Then increment `depth` by 1.
If `ch == ')'`: decrement `depth` by 1 first. Then check if `depth > 0`. If true, append `ch` to `res`.
Join and return `res` as a single string.

find-the-maximum-number-of-elements-in-s.title: Find the Maximum Number of Elements in Subset
find-the-maximum-number-of-elements-in-s.insight: For any base x > 1, repeated squaring grows at a double-exponential rate: 2, 4, 16, 256, 65536, >10^9. That means any valid chain has at most 5 distinct values, bounding the simulation for each number to O(log log(max_val)) steps. The only trap is x = 1, because 1 squared stays 1, which simply allows us to take the largest odd count of 1s.
find-the-maximum-number-of-elements-in-s.approach:
Count the frequency of each number using a hash map.
Initialise the result with the special case for 1: if 1 is present, take the largest odd count (count if odd, count - 1 if even); otherwise default to 1.
Iterate through each unique key x > 1 present in the map.
For the current x, track chain length starting at 0 and set curr = x.
While count[curr] >= 2, add 2 to the chain length and advance curr to curr * curr.
Once the loop terminates, check curr: if count[curr] >= 1, we can use it as our peak element, so add 1.
If count[curr] == 0, the last paired element must become the peak instead, so subtract 1 from the chain length.
Update the global maximum with this chain's length, then return the maximum after checking all keys.
find-the-maximum-number-of-elements-in-s.solution:
from collections import Counter

class Solution:
    def maximumLength(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        counts = Counter(nums)
        
        # Base case: any single element gives length 1
        ans = 1
        
        # Special case: 1s can form a chain of any odd length
        if 1 in counts:
            ones = counts[1]
            ans = max(ans, ones if ones % 2 != 0 else ones - 1)
        
        # Check squaring chains for all x > 1
        for x in counts:
            if x == 1:
                continue
            
            length = 0
            curr = x
            
            # We need pairs of each intermediate level
            while counts.get(curr, 0) >= 2:
                length += 2
                curr = curr * curr
            
            # If the next square exists at least once, it's the peak
            if counts.get(curr, 0) >= 1:
                length += 1
            else:
                # Otherwise, one copy of the last doubled number acts as the peak
                length -= 1
            
            ans = max(ans, length)
            
        return ans

circular-array-loop.title: Circular Array Loop
circular-array-loop.insight: Because each index has exactly one deterministic outgoing jump, this is a directed functional graph. We can run slow and fast pointers per component. The trick to hitting O(n) time and O(1) space is that whenever a path changes direction or hits a 1-element loop, the entire path is a dead end — so we do a quick second pass along that path turning elements to 0 so we never visit them again.
circular-array-loop.approach:
1. Define a helper `getNext(i)` returning `((i + nums[i]) % n + n) % n` to ensure a positive wrapped index.
2. Loop `i` from `0` to `n - 1`. If `nums[i] == 0`, skip it because it's already a proven dead end.
3. Set `slow = i`, `fast = i`, and record `isForward = (nums[i] > 0)`.
4. In a `while` loop, validate slow's next step and both of fast's next two steps against `isForward`.
5. If any step flips sign or hits a zero, break out of the pointer chase.
6. Advance `slow` by 1 hop and `fast` by 2 hops. If `slow == fast`, check if `slow == getNext(slow)`; if not a self-loop, return `true`.
7. If the chase broke without a valid cycle, trace from `i` again, setting each element with matching direction to `0` until direction changes or `0` is reached.
8. If the outer loop finishes without finding any valid cycle, return `false`.

find-players-with-zero-or-one-losses.title: Find Players With Zero or One Losses
find-players-with-zero-or-one-losses.insight: Every player who took part is either a winner, a loser, or both. We can record match outcomes in a single pass using a hash map mapping player ID to their total losses: if a winner isn't in the map yet, record 0 losses; if a loser is encountered, increment their loss count (or initialise it to 1). Once populated, we just partition the keys by loss count.
find-players-with-zero-or-one-losses.approach:
Create a hash map `loss_count` to map player ID to number of defeats.
Iterate through each match `[winner, loser]` in `matches`.
If `winner` is not in `loss_count`, set `loss_count[winner] = 0`.
Increment `loss_count[loser]` by 1, initialising from 0 if not present.
Initialise two lists: `zero_loss` and `one_loss`.
Iterate over `player, count` in `loss_count.items()`.
If `count == 0`, append `player` to `zero_loss`; if `count == 1`, append to `one_loss`.
Sort both lists in ascending order and return `[zero_loss, one_loss]`.

word-pattern.title: Word Pattern
word-pattern.insight: A valid pattern requires a bijection: every pattern character maps to exactly one word, and every word maps to exactly one pattern character. If we only track `char -> word`, cases like `pattern = 'ab', s = 'dog dog'` slip through. We must check both directions simultaneously, either with two dictionaries or one dictionary plus a seen set.
word-pattern.approach:
Split string s into a list of words using space as the delimiter.
If len(pattern) != len(words), immediately return False.
Initialise two hash maps: char_to_word and word_to_char.
Iterate through zipped pairs of (char, word).
If char is in char_to_word and char_to_word[char] != word, return False.
If word is in word_to_char and word_to_char[word] != char, return False.
Record char_to_word[char] = word and word_to_char[word] = char.
If the loop completes without mismatches, return True.

find-all-lonely-numbers-in-the-array.title: Find All Lonely Numbers in the Array
find-all-lonely-numbers-in-the-array.insight: A number's eligibility depends purely on counts: its own count must be exactly one, and the counts of x - 1 and x + 1 must both be zero. By building a frequency map in one pass, we can test all three conditions in O(1) time per distinct number in a second pass.
find-all-lonely-numbers-in-the-array.approach:
Initialise an empty hash map (or Counter) to track frequencies of each number.
Iterate through nums once to populate the frequency map.
Initialise an empty results list 'lonely'.
Iterate over the unique keys (or elements) in the frequency map.
For each number x, check if its frequency is strictly equal to 1.
If it is, check whether neither (x - 1) nor (x + 1) exists in the frequency map.
If all conditions hold, append x to the results list.
Return the results list.

number-of-good-paths.title: Number of Good Paths
number-of-good-paths.insight: If we introduce nodes in non-decreasing order of their values, any connected component formed so far only contains nodes with value at most v. So when we process all nodes of value v and connect them to their valid neighbours, all nodes with value v falling into the same DSU component can freely reach each other. For a component with k nodes of value v, that gives exactly k * (k - 1) / 2 new paths.
number-of-good-paths.approach:
1. Initialise the answer to n because every single node is a good path.
2. Build an adjacency list for the tree.
3. Group node indices by their value into a sorted dictionary or bucket array.
4. Implement a standard DSU (Disjoint Set Union) with path compression and union by rank.
5. Iterate through the distinct values in ascending order.
6. For each node u with current value v, check each neighbour nei; if vals[nei] <= v, union u and nei.
7. Once all unions for value v are done, find the DSU leader (root) for each node of value v.
8. Count the frequency of each root among nodes with value v using a hash map.
9. For each root with count c, add c * (c - 1) // 2 to the answer.
10. Return the total answer after all values are processed.

integer-break.title: Integer Break
integer-break.insight: Mathematically, maximizing (n/x)^x leads to x = e ≈ 2.718, making 3 the optimal integer factor. Furthermore, 3 * 3 > 2 * 2 * 2 for a sum of 6 (9 vs 8), so 3s always beat 2s. Any factor 4 or larger can be broken into smaller numbers without losing product (e.g., 4 = 2*2, 5 < 2*3), so we only ever want 2s and 3s, prioritizing 3s.
integer-break.approach:
1. Handle the forced small-number edge cases: if n == 2 return 1 (1+1), if n == 3 return 2 (1+2).
2. Initialise a variable `product = 1` to accumulate our factors.
3. Enter a loop while n > 4.
4. In each iteration, multiply `product` by 3 and decrement `n` by 3.
5. When n <= 4, multiply `product` by whatever is left in `n` (which will be 2, 3, or 4).
6. Return `product`.

minimum-score-of-a-path-between-two-citi.title: Minimum Score of a Path Between Two Cities
minimum-score-of-a-path-between-two-citi.insight: Since you can re-use roads and revisit cities freely, you don't actually need a simple path. If any edge exists inside the connected component containing city 1, you can simply take a detour to that edge, cross it, cross back, and proceed to city n. Thus, the minimum score of a path from 1 to n is simply the minimum weight among all edges reachable from city 1.
minimum-score-of-a-path-between-two-citi.approach:
1. Build an adjacency list where each node points to (neighbour, distance) pairs.
2. Initialise a visited set and a variable min_score to infinity.
3. Start a BFS or DFS from node 1.
4. For the current node, mark it as visited.
5. Iterate through all outgoing edges (neighbour, distance).
6. Update min_score = min(min_score, distance).
7. If the neighbour hasn't been visited yet, push it to the queue/stack and mark as visited.
8. When the traversal finishes, return min_score.

find-greatest-common-divisor-of-array.title: Find Greatest Common Divisor of Array
find-greatest-common-divisor-of-array.insight: The entire problem reduces to finding two numbers — the global minimum and maximum — and applying Euclid's algorithm. Euclid's algorithm works on the principle that gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b), which runs in logarithmic time with respect to the smaller integer.
find-greatest-common-divisor-of-array.approach:
1. Initialise min_val to infinity and max_val to -infinity (or use the first element).
2. Iterate through every number x in nums.
3. Update min_val = min(min_val, x) and max_val = max(max_val, x).
4. Set up Euclid's algorithm with a = max_val and b = min_val.
5. Loop while b is not zero: compute remainder = a % b, set a = b, and b = remainder.
6. Return a as the greatest common divisor.

number-of-paths-with-max-score.title: Number of Paths with Max Score
number-of-paths-with-max-score.insight: Notice the directions form a DAG directed towards (0, 0). Any cell's optimal path only depends on three incoming neighbours: down (r+1, c), right (r, c+1), and diagonal (r+1, c+1). By storing a pair (max_score, ways) at each cell and iterating backwards from (n-1, n-1) to (0, 0), we find the global max score and sum the ways of all transitions that achieve that maximum.
number-of-paths-with-max-score.approach:
Define MOD = 10**9 + 7 and size n = len(board).
Create two 2D arrays (or a single array of pairs): dp_score and dp_count of size n x n, initialised to -1 and 0 respectively.
Set the base case at the starting cell: dp_score[n-1][n-1] = 0 and dp_count[n-1][n-1] = 1.
Iterate r from n-1 down to 0, and c from n-1 down to 0.
Skip the bottom-right starting square, and skip any cell containing 'X'.
Inspect the three possible predecessors: (r+1, c), (r, c+1), and (r+1, c+1).
Find the maximum score among reachable predecessors (those with dp_count > 0).
If at least one neighbour is reachable, sum the dp_counts of all predecessors matching that maximum score modulo MOD.
Add the current cell's digit (or 0 if it is 'E') to this maximum score to form dp_score[r][c].
After the loops finish, check dp_count[0][0]; return [dp_score[0][0], dp_count[0][0]] if dp_count[0][0] > 0 else [0, 0].

average-time-of-process-per-machine.title: Average Time of Process per Machine
average-time-of-process-per-machine.insight: Because each process has exactly two rows—one 'start' and one 'end'—we can self-join the table `a` (start) and `b` (end) on matching `machine_id` and `process_id`. The duration is simply `b.timestamp - a.timestamp`, and averaging that per `machine_id` directly gives the answer without tricky window functions.
average-time-of-process-per-machine.approach:
1. Alias the Activity table as `a` for start records (`a.activity_type = 'start'`).
2. Alias the Activity table as `b` for end records (`b.activity_type = 'end'`).
3. Join `a` and `b` on `a.machine_id = b.machine_id` AND `a.process_id = b.process_id`.
4. For each joined row, compute the elapsed time as `b.timestamp - a.timestamp`.
5. Group the result set by `a.machine_id`.
6. Apply `AVG(b.timestamp - a.timestamp)` to compute the mean process duration per machine.
7. Wrap the average in `ROUND(..., 3)` and alias as `processing_time`.
8. Select `a.machine_id` alongside `processing_time`.
average-time-of-process-per-machine.solution:
# Write your MySQL query statement below
# Using self-join to pair start and end timestamps
SELECT 
    a.machine_id,
    ROUND(AVG(b.timestamp - a.timestamp), 3) AS processing_time
FROM Activity a
JOIN Activity b
    ON a.machine_id = b.machine_id
   AND a.process_id = b.process_id
   AND a.activity_type = 'start'
   AND b.activity_type = 'end'
GROUP BY a.machine_id;

longest-increasing-subsequence-ii.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence II
longest-increasing-subsequence-ii.insight: Unlike standard LIS where patience sorting works because smaller tails always dominate, the upper bound window of size k breaks monotonicity. But notice that for a current value x, the previous valid value must lie strictly in the value range [x - k, x - 1]. This turns our DP transition into a classic Range Maximum Query over value space, which an iterative segment tree resolves and updates in O(log M) per element.
longest-increasing-subsequence-ii.approach:
1. Find the maximum value M in nums to define the segment tree size (or fix to 10^5).
2. Initialise an iterative segment tree of size 2 * (M + 1) filled with zeros.
3. Define a query(left, right) function that traverses bottom-up to return the maximum value in [left, right].
4. Define an update(idx, val) function that updates the leaf at idx and refreshes parent nodes.
5. Iterate through each number x in nums.
6. Calculate the valid predecessor range: L = max(1, x - k) and R = x - 1.
7. If L <= R, query the tree for the maximum DP value best_prev in [L, R]; otherwise best_prev = 0.
8. Update the tree at position x with best_prev + 1.
9. After processing all elements, return the global maximum in the tree (which is tree[1] or max over all queries).

count-number-of-nice-subarrays.title: Count Number of Nice Subarrays
count-number-of-nice-subarrays.insight: Counting subarrays with *exactly* k odds is messy because even numbers let you expand or shrink without changing the odd tally. However, counting subarrays with *at most* k odds is strictly monotonic: expanding right adds odds, shrinking left removes them, and every valid window [left, right] contributes exactly `right - left + 1` subarrays. Because `exact(k) = atMost(k) - atMost(k - 1)`, we can solve it with one simple, reusable helper.
count-number-of-nice-subarrays.approach:
1. Define a helper `at_most(goal)` returning the number of subarrays with at most `goal` odd numbers.
2. Inside `at_most`, immediately return 0 if `goal < 0` to guard against `k - 1` when k is 0.
3. Initialise `left = 0`, `odds = 0`, and `res = 0`.
4. Iterate `right` through `0` to `len(nums) - 1`.
5. Increment `odds` if the current element is odd (`nums[right] & 1`).
6. While `odds > goal`, decrement `odds` if `nums[left]` is odd and increment `left`.
7. Accumulate `right - left + 1` into `res` (each step adds all valid subarrays ending at `right`).
8. In the main function, return `at_most(k) - at_most(k - 1)`.

find-leaves-of-binary-tree.title: Find Leaves of Binary Tree
find-leaves-of-binary-tree.insight: A node's removal round is simply its distance (height) from the furthest descendant leaf. A leaf has height 0 (index 0). Any parent node has height = 1 + max(left_height, right_height). If we compute this bottom-up in a single post-order traversal, a node with height `h` belongs to the `h`-th sub-array in our final output.
find-leaves-of-binary-tree.approach:
Initialise an empty list of lists `result` to hold the leaf layers.
Define a helper function `getHeight(node)` that returns an integer representing the node's height from the bottom.
Base case: if `node` is `null`, return -1.
Recursively compute `leftHeight = getHeight(node.left)` and `rightHeight = getHeight(node.right)`.
Compute `currHeight = 1 + max(leftHeight, rightHeight)`.
If `currHeight == len(result)`, append a new empty list to `result` to accommodate this new layer.
Append `node.val` to `result[currHeight]`.
Return `currHeight` up to the caller.
Call `getHeight(root)` from the main function and return `result`.
find-leaves-of-binary-tree.solution:
# Definition for a binary tree node.
# class TreeNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.left = left
#         self.right = right

class Solution:
    def findLeaves(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> List[List[int]]:
        result = []

        def get_height(node: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
            if not node:
                return -1
            
            left_h = get_height(node.left)
            right_h = get_height(node.right)
            curr_h = 1 + max(left_h, right_h)
            
            # Expand result list if this is the first node at this height
            if curr_h == len(result):
                result.append([])
            
            result[curr_h].append(node.val)
            return curr_h

        get_height(root)
        return result

minimum-path-sum.title: Minimum Path Sum
minimum-path-sum.insight: Every cell (r, c) can only be entered from (r-1, c) or (r, c-1). This gives the recurrence dp[r][c] = grid[r][c] + min(dp[r-1][c], dp[r][c-1]). Notice we only ever need values from the current row and the row directly above, meaning we can collapse the DP table into a single 1D array of length n.
minimum-path-sum.approach:
1. Grab dimensions m and n; initialise a 1D DP array of size n with infinity.
2. Set dp[0] = 0 as the virtual entry point before the start cell.
3. First pass on row 0: compute prefix sums so each cell holds the cumulative cost from the left.
4. For each subsequent row r from 1 to m - 1:
5. Update dp[0] += grid[r][0] since the first column can only come from directly above.
6. Iterate column c from 1 to n - 1: update dp[c] = grid[r][c] + min(dp[c], dp[c - 1]), where dp[c] is the cell above and dp[c-1] is the cell to the left.
7. After processing all rows, return dp[-1].
minimum-path-sum.solution:
class Solution:
    def minPathSum(self, grid: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        m, n = len(grid), len(grid[0])
        
        # 1D DP array representing the minimum path to each cell in the current row
        dp = [0] * n
        dp[0] = grid[0][0]
        
        # Initialize first row (can only come from the left)
        for c in range(1, n):
            dp[c] = dp[c - 1] + grid[0][c]
            
        # Process remaining rows
        for r in range(1, m):
            dp[0] += grid[r][0]  # First column can only come from above
            for c in range(1, n):
                # dp[c] currently holds the value from row r-1 (above)
                # dp[c-1] holds the newly computed value from row r (left)
                dp[c] = grid[r][c] + min(dp[c], dp[c - 1])
                
        return dp[-1]

evaluate-reverse-polish-notation.title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
evaluate-reverse-polish-notation.insight: RPN evaluates operators strictly against the most recently encountered operands. A Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) stack holds pending operands so that whenever an operator arrives, the required operands are sitting right at the top in O(1) time.
evaluate-reverse-polish-notation.approach:
Initialise an empty stack to hold integer operands.
Loop over each string token in the input list.
If the token is an operator (+, -, *, /), pop the top element as b (right operand) and the next as a (left operand).
Apply the operation: compute a + b, a - b, a * b, or int(a / b) for division.
Push the resulting integer back onto the stack.
If the token is a number, parse it as an integer and push it onto the stack.
After exhausting all tokens, the stack will contain exactly one element.
Pop and return that final element as the result.

find-words-containing-character.title: Find Words Containing Character
find-words-containing-character.insight: Because we only need to know whether the character exists in a string, we can do a linear scan with an early exit as soon as we see the first match. There's no complex data structure needed given the problem constraints.
find-words-containing-character.approach:
Initialise an empty list or dynamic array called result.
Iterate through the words array using index i from 0 up to words.length - 1.
Check if character x exists in words[i] using an in-operator or indexOf search.
If x is found, append index i to result.
Continue to the next word immediately without checking remaining characters of current word.
Return result after inspecting all words.

smallest-even-multiple.title: Smallest Even Multiple
smallest-even-multiple.insight: We are looking for LCM(2, n). Since 2 is prime, gcd(2, n) is either 2 (when n is even) or 1 (when n is odd). Therefore, LCM(2, n) = (2 * n) / gcd(2, n), which simplifies immediately to n if n is even, and 2n if n is odd.
smallest-even-multiple.approach:
1. Inspect the parity of n using n % 2 or bitwise n & 1.
2. If n is even (n % 2 == 0), n is already a multiple of 2 and itself.
3. Return n directly in this case.
4. If n is odd, the smallest multiple sharing both factors is 2 * n.
5. Return 2 * n.
6. Optionally express this cleanly as `return n if n % 2 == 0 else 2 * n` or bitwise `return n << (n & 1)`.

n-th-tribonacci-number.title: N-th Tribonacci Number
n-th-tribonacci-number.insight: To calculate T(i), we only ever need the values of T(i-3), T(i-2), and T(i-1). We do not need an array of size n + 1 or size 38; maintaining three variables `a`, `b`, and `c` and updating them in a single tuple assignment `a, b, c = b, c, a + b + c` gives an optimal O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space solution.
n-th-tribonacci-number.approach:
Check base cases: if n == 0, return 0 immediately.
If n == 1 or n == 2, return 1 immediately.
Initialise three state variables representing the first three numbers: a = 0, b = 1, c = 1.
Loop from index 3 up to n (inclusive), running n - 2 times.
In each iteration, compute the next term next_val = a + b + c.
Shift the window by updating: a = b, b = c, c = next_val (or simultaneously via tuple unpacking).
After the loop finishes, c holds the value of T(n).
Return c.

counter.title: Counter
counter.insight: By returning an inner function that closes over the outer scope's variable, each instance encapsulates its own state independently. In languages like Python, we use the 'nonlocal' keyword, or post-increment semantics in JavaScript/Java to return the current value before bumping it.
counter.approach:
1. Define the outer factory function that accepts the starting integer n.
2. Initialise an internal state variable to n (or reuse n directly in languages that permit it).
3. Define the inner counter function that accesses this outer state.
4. Inside the inner function, record the current value to return.
5. Increment the internal state by 1.
6. Return the recorded value.
7. Return the inner function object from the outer factory function.
counter.solution:
from typing import Callable

def createCounter(n: int) -> Callable[[], int]:
    # Track the current count in the outer closure scope
    val = n
    
    def counter() -> int:
        nonlocal val
        res = val
        val += 1
        return res
        
    return counter

duplicate-zeros.title: Duplicate Zeros
duplicate-zeros.insight: Writing forwards causes newly duplicated zeros to overwrite downstream elements before we can read them. If we first find the effective boundary of elements that will actually survive in the final array, we can write from back to front into their final destination safely.
duplicate-zeros.approach:
1. Count how many zeros can be duplicated without exceeding the array boundary `n - 1`.
2. Maintain `possible_dups = 0` and iterate `i` from 0 upwards.
3. Stop iterating once `i > n - 1 - possible_dups`.
4. Handle the edge case: if `i == n - 1 - possible_dups` and `arr[i] == 0`, this boundary zero can only be copied once; write `arr[n - 1] = 0` and decrement the boundary/effective length.
5. Set a read pointer `last = n - 1 - possible_dups` (or after edge check).
6. Iterate `i` from `last` down to 0, writing to `i + possible_dups`.
7. If `arr[i] == 0`, write 0 at `i + possible_dups`, decrement `possible_dups`, and write another 0 at `i + possible_dups`.
8. If `arr[i] != 0`, copy `arr[i]` directly to `arr[i + possible_dups]`.
duplicate-zeros.solution:
class Solution:
    def duplicateZeros(self, arr: list[int]) -> None:
        """
        Do not return anything, modify arr in-place instead.
        """
        n = len(arr)
        possible_dups = 0
        length_ = n - 1

        # Find the number of zeros that will fit in the modified array
        i = 0
        while i <= length_ - possible_dups:
            if arr[i] == 0:
                # Edge case: zero on the boundary that cannot be duplicated
                if i == length_ - possible_dups:
                    arr[length_] = 0
                    length_ -= 1
                    break
                possible_dups += 1
            i += 1

        # Copy elements working backwards
        last = length_ - possible_dups
        for j in range(last, -1, -1):
            if arr[j] == 0:
                arr[j + possible_dups] = 0
                possible_dups -= 1
                arr[j + possible_dups] = 0
            else:
                arr[j + possible_dups] = arr[j]

maximum-absolute-sum-of-any-subarray.title: Maximum Absolute Sum of Any Subarray
maximum-absolute-sum-of-any-subarray.insight: Taking the absolute value |x| means we're looking for either the most positive subarray sum or the most negative subarray sum. Because Kadane's algorithm gives us the maximum subarray sum in O(n) time, we can simply run it twice simultaneously — once tracking the running maximum subarray sum and once tracking the running minimum subarray sum. The answer is max(max_sum, abs(min_sum)).
maximum-absolute-sum-of-any-subarray.approach:
Initialize two running trackers: `current_max = 0` and `current_min = 0`.
Initialize two global extreme trackers: `max_sum = 0` and `min_sum = 0`.
Iterate through each number `x` in `nums`.
Update `current_max` to `max(x, current_max + x)` (or `max(0, current_max) + x`).
Update `current_min` to `min(x, current_min + x)` (or `min(0, current_min) + x`).
Update `max_sum = max(max_sum, current_max)` and `min_sum = min(min_sum, current_min)`.
After the loop, return `max(max_sum, abs(min_sum))`.
maximum-absolute-sum-of-any-subarray.solution:
class Solution:
    def maxAbsoluteSum(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        max_sum = 0
        min_sum = 0
        cur_max = 0
        cur_min = 0
        
        for x in nums:
            # Kadane's for max subarray sum
            cur_max = max(x, cur_max + x)
            max_sum = max(max_sum, cur_max)
            
            # Kadane's for min subarray sum
            cur_min = min(x, cur_min + x)
            min_sum = min(min_sum, cur_min)
            
        return max(max_sum, abs(min_sum))

count-the-number-of-consistent-strings.title: Count the Number of Consistent Strings
count-the-number-of-consistent-strings.insight: Because the alphabet is just 26 lowercase English letters, we can represent allowed as a 26-bit integer mask or a fixed-size boolean array/hash set. Checking if a word is consistent reduces to verifying that every character's bit is active in our allowed mask.
count-the-number-of-consistent-strings.approach:
Initialise an integer bitmask `allowed_mask = 0` and a counter `count = 0`.
Iterate through each character in `allowed` and set the corresponding bit: `allowed_mask |= 1 << (ord(c) - ord('a'))`.
Iterate through each word in `words`.
For the current word, check each character to see if its bit is missing in `allowed_mask` (i.e. `((allowed_mask >> bit) & 1) == 0`).
If any character is missing, mark the word as inconsistent and break early.
If the loop finishes without finding an invalid character, increment `count`.
Return `count` after inspecting all words.

nim-game.title: Nim Game
nim-game.insight: If n is 1, 2, or 3, you win immediately. If n is 4, whatever you take (1, 2, or 3), your opponent faces 3, 2, or 1 and wins. Hence, 4 is a guaranteed losing state. For n = 5, 6, 7, you can take 1, 2, or 3 stones respectively to hand your opponent 4 stones, guaranteeing your win. This cycle repeats every 4 stones: any multiple of 4 is a losing state because any move you make hands a non-multiple of 4 back to your opponent.
nim-game.approach:
1. Note the base cases: n in {1, 2, 3} are winning positions (take all).
2. Identify n = 4 as a losing position (whatever you take, opponent takes the rest).
3. Observe that from n = 5, 6, 7, you can transition to 4 by taking 1, 2, or 3 stones.
4. Observe that from n = 8, any move lands on 5, 6, or 7, which are all winning positions for the opponent, making 8 a losing position.
5. Conclude inductively that position n is a losing position if and only if n % 4 == 0.
6. Return the boolean result of checking whether n % 4 != 0.

super-pow.title: Super Pow
super-pow.insight: We can evaluate the exponent using Horner's method on digits. If our current accumulated power represents a prefix exponent P, appending a new digit d means the new exponent is 10*P + d. By exponent rules, a^(10*P + d) = (a^P)^10 * a^d. Doing this modulo 1337 at every step keeps all intermediate values strictly under 1337.
super-pow.approach:
Set modulus M = 1337 and pre-reduce a = a % M.
Initialize result accumulator ans = 1.
Define or use modular exponentiation pow(base, exp, M).
Loop through each digit d in array b from left to right.
Update ans = (pow(ans, 10, M) * pow(a, d, M)) % M.
After processing all digits in b, return ans.

scramble-string.title: Scramble String
scramble-string.insight: Any scramble operation splits s1 into length k and n-k. For a valid scramble to exist, either s1[:k] matches s2[:k] and s1[k:] matches s2[k:] (no swap), OR s1[:k] matches s2[n-k:] and s1[k:] matches s2[:n-k] (swapped). Crucially, s1 and s2 must always be anagrams, so checking character counts lets us prune invalid recursive branches immediately, and memoizing (s1, s2) prevents re-evaluating shared sub-states.
scramble-string.approach:
1. Define a recursive helper or use @lru_cache on `isScramble(s1, s2)`.
2. Base case: if `s1 == s2`, return True immediately.
3. Pruning: check if `Counter(s1) == Counter(s2)`; if not, return False.
4. Let n be the length of s1.
5. Iterate split length k from 1 to n - 1.
6. Check unswapped case: `isScramble(s1[:k], s2[:k]) and isScramble(s1[k:], s2[k:])`. If True, return True.
7. Check swapped case: `isScramble(s1[:k], s2[n-k:]) and isScramble(s1[k:], s2[:n-k])`. If True, return True.
8. If no split yields True across all 1 to n - 1, return False.
9. Cache the boolean result for the pair `(s1, s2)`.

k-items-with-the-maximum-sum.title: K Items With the Maximum Sum
k-items-with-the-maximum-sum.insight: Since we only have three distinct values (1, 0, -1), their optimal order is already known: always favour 1 over 0, and 0 over -1. We can break the decision into three straightforward thresholds: if k fits within the 1s, return k; if k extends into the 0s, the sum caps at numOnes; if k spills over into the -1s, subtract the remainder from numOnes.
k-items-with-the-maximum-sum.approach:
1. Check if k <= numOnes. If so, return k immediately because we can take purely 1s.
2. If k > numOnes, check if k <= numOnes + numZeros.
3. If so, we exhaust all 1s and pad the rest with 0s, so the sum is numOnes.
4. If k exceeds numOnes + numZeros, we are forced to pick some -1s.
5. Calculate the remaining items we must pick: rem = k - (numOnes + numZeros).
6. Subtract rem from numOnes to account for the -1s chosen.
7. Return the resulting sum.

partition-labels.title: Partition Labels
partition-labels.insight: A partition can only safely end when we've reached an index that is at or past the final occurrence of every character encountered so far. By precomputing each letter's final index in a hash map, we turn boundary extension into a single linear sweep where the boundary is just the running maximum of those final positions.
partition-labels.approach:
First pass: populate a lookup table `last_seen` mapping each distinct character to its rightmost index in `s`.
Initialise two pointer variables: `start = 0` for the current segment's start, and `end = 0` for its required end boundary.
Initialise an empty list `ans` to store the segment sizes.
Second pass: iterate through `s` with index `i` and character `ch`.
Update `end = max(end, last_seen[ch])` to ensure the current boundary covers this character's final appearance.
If the current index `i` equals `end`, we've captured all characters belonging exclusively to this chunk.
Append the chunk length `end - start + 1` to `ans`, then set `start = i + 1` for the next chunk.
Return `ans` once the loop terminates.

vertical-order-traversal-of-a-binary-tre.title: Vertical Order Traversal of a Binary Tree
vertical-order-traversal-of-a-binary-tre.insight: Every node's position is completely determined by (col, row). If we bucket nodes into a hash map by `col` and sort only the `(row, val)` pairs within each column (or use BFS to keep rows naturally monotonic, only sorting overlaps at identical row and col), we keep the coordinate logic modular and straightforward.
vertical-order-traversal-of-a-binary-tre.approach:
1. Use a hash map mapping `col -> list of (row, val)` and track `min_col` and `max_col` boundaries.
2. Run a standard BFS queue initialised with `(root, 0, 0)` representing `(node, row, col)`.
3. While the queue isn't empty, pop `(node, row, col)` and append `(row, node.val)` to `map[col]`.
4. Push left child with `(row + 1, col - 1)` and right child with `(row + 1, col + 1)`.
5. Update `min_col = min(min_col, col)` and `max_col = max(max_col, col)` during traversal.
6. Iterate `c` from `min_col` to `max_col`, sort each column's list by `(row, val)`.
7. Extract just the node values from the sorted column list and append to `result`.
8. Return `result`.
vertical-order-traversal-of-a-binary-tre.time: O(N log(N / K)) on average where K is the number of columns, O(N log N) worst-case if all nodes share a column.
vertical-order-traversal-of-a-binary-tre.solution:
# Definition for a binary tree node.
# class TreeNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.left = left
#         self.right = right

from collections import defaultdict, deque
from typing import Optional, List

class Solution:
    def verticalTraversal(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> List[List[int]]:
        if not root:
            return []
        
        # Map col -> list of (row, val)
        col_map = defaultdict(list)
        queue = deque([(root, 0, 0)])  # (node, row, col)
        min_col = max_col = 0
        
        while queue:
            node, row, col = queue.popleft()
            col_map[col].append((row, node.val))
            min_col = min(min_col, col)
            max_col = max(max_col, col)
            
            if node.left:
                queue.append((node.left, row + 1, col - 1))
            if node.right:
                queue.append((node.right, row + 1, col + 1))
        
        res = []
        # Iterate columns from leftmost to rightmost
        for c in range(min_col, max_col + 1):
            # Sort primarily by row, secondarily by value
            col_map[c].sort(key=lambda x: (x[0], x[1]))
            res.append([val for _, val in col_map[c]])
            
        return res

maximum-number-of-events-that-can-be-att.title: Maximum Number of Events That Can Be Attended
maximum-number-of-events-that-can-be-att.insight: On any given day, if multiple available events are ongoing, it's always optimal to attend the one that ends first. Any event ending later gives us greater flexibility to attend on future days. We can simulate day by day, pushing open events into a min-heap of end dates, popping expired ones, and picking the earliest deadline.
maximum-number-of-events-that-can-be-att.approach:
1. Sort the events list in ascending order based on startDay.
2. Initialise a min-heap `min_heap` to store active event end days, a counter `ans = 0`, an index `i = 0`, and `day = 0`.
3. Loop while there are unprocessed events (`i < len(events)`) or active events in `min_heap`.
4. If `min_heap` is empty, fast-forward `day` to `events[i][0]` to skip idle days.
5. Push all events starting on `day` onto `min_heap` (storing their `endDay`), advancing `i`.
6. Discard any events from `min_heap` that have already expired (where `endDay < day`).
7. If `min_heap` is not empty, pop the smallest `endDay` (attend this event), increment `ans`, and increment `day` by 1.
maximum-number-of-events-that-can-be-att.solution:
import heapq

class Solution:
    def maxEvents(self, events: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        # Sort events by their start day
        events.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
        
        min_heap = []  # Stores end days of currently available events
        ans = 0
        i = 0
        n = len(events)
        day = 0
        
        while i < n or min_heap:
            # If no active events, jump straight to the next event's start day
            if not min_heap:
                day = events[i][0]
            
            # Add all events starting on the current day to the heap
            while i < n and events[i][0] <= day:
                heapq.heappush(min_heap, events[i][1])
                i += 1
            
            # Remove events that have already ended
            while min_heap and min_heap[0] < day:
                heapq.heappop(min_heap)
            
            # Attend the event ending earliest
            if min_heap:
                heapq.heappop(min_heap)
                ans += 1
                day += 1
                
        return ans

ipo.title: IPO
ipo.insight: Because profits are non-negative, our total capital w only ever increases. This monotonicity means once a project becomes affordable, it remains affordable forever; we can sort all projects by required capital once, move affordable ones into a max-heap as w grows, and always pop the largest profit.
ipo.approach:
1. Pair each project's capital and profit together as tuples `(capital[i], profits[i])`.
2. Sort the project pairs in ascending order of their required capital.
3. Initialise a max-heap to store the profits of currently affordable projects.
4. Maintain a pointer `ptr = 0` to track our progress through the sorted projects list.
5. Loop up to `k` times: while `ptr < n` and `projects[ptr].capital <= w`, push `projects[ptr].profit` into the max-heap, then increment `ptr`.
6. If the max-heap is empty, break early since we cannot afford any more projects.
7. Pop the maximum profit from the heap and add it to `w`.
8. After `k` iterations (or early termination), return `w`.
ipo.time: O(n log n + k log n)
ipo.solution:
import heapq

class Solution:
    def findMaximizedCapital(self, k: int, w: int, profits: list[int], capital: list[int]) -> int:
        n = len(profits)
        # Pair and sort by capital requirement ascending
        projects = sorted(zip(capital, profits))
        
        max_profit_heap = []
        ptr = 0
        
        for _ in range(k):
            # Push all projects we can afford with current capital
            while ptr < n and projects[ptr][0] <= w:
                # Python heapq is a min-heap, invert profit to simulate max-heap
                heapq.heappush(max_profit_heap, -projects[ptr][1])
                ptr += 1
            
            # If no affordable projects left, we can't proceed
            if not max_profit_heap:
                break
            
            # Greedily take the most profitable project
            w += -heapq.heappop(max_profit_heap)
            
        return w

maximum-candies-allocated-to-k-children.title: Maximum Candies Allocated to K Children
maximum-candies-allocated-to-k-children.insight: The problem has a monotonic property: if we can successfully give every child c candies, we can definitely give them c - 1 candies. That lets us discard the linear scan and binary search over the answer range [1, max(candies)], taking only about 24 iterations.
maximum-candies-allocated-to-k-children.approach:
First, check if the total sum of candies is less than k; if so, immediately return 0.
Initialise the binary search bounds: low = 1 and high = max(candies).
Maintain a variable ans = 0 to store the largest valid pile size found.
While low <= high, calculate mid = (low + high) // 2.
Count the total sub-piles of size mid by computing sum(c // mid for c in candies).
If the total sub-piles >= k, mid is achievable: set ans = mid and push low = mid + 1 to try for more.
If the total sub-piles < k, mid is too large: shrink the search space with high = mid - 1.
Return ans once low exceeds high.

rank-scores.title: Rank Scores
rank-scores.insight: The requirement 'ties share rank, no holes between consecutive ranks' is literally DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) in SQL, or `rank(method='dense', ascending=False)` in Pandas.
rank-scores.approach:
1. Check if the input DataFrame is empty; if so, return columns ['score', 'rank'].
2. Use the built-in `rank` method on the 'score' column.
3. Set `method='dense'` to ensure ties get identical ranks without skips.
4. Set `ascending=False` so higher scores receive lower numeric ranks (1, 2, ...).
5. Cast the resulting rank column to integer if needed.
6. Sort the resulting table by 'score' descending.
7. Project only the ['score', 'rank'] columns and return.

shortest-palindrome.title: Shortest Palindrome
shortest-palindrome.insight: Any palindrome formed by prepending characters looks like reverse(suffix) + longest_palindromic_prefix + suffix. So the problem boils down to finding the longest palindromic prefix of s. That's equivalent to finding the longest prefix of s that matches a suffix of reverse(s). If we build temp = s + '#' + reverse(s), the standard KMP prefix function (LPS array) evaluated at the very last index gives us this exact length in linear time.
shortest-palindrome.approach:
Check if s is empty; if so, return s.
Store rev_s = s[::-1].
Construct the combined string concat = s + '#' + rev_s. The '#' acts as a sentinel so the prefix match cannot exceed len(s).
Initialise an LPS (longest prefix-suffix) array pi of length len(concat) with zeros.
Use two pointers, i from 1 to len(concat)-1 and j = 0, to populate pi using standard KMP failure function logic.
When characters match, increment j and set pi[i] = j. When they mismatch and j > 0, fallback to j = pi[j - 1].
The value pi[-1] is the length k of the longest palindromic prefix in s.
Extract the un-matched suffix from the original string, reverse it (which is rev_s[:len(s) - k]), and prepend it to s.

smallest-palindromic-rearrangement-ii.title: Smallest Palindromic Rearrangement II
smallest-palindromic-rearrangement-ii.insight: A palindrome of length N is completely determined by its first floor(N / 2) characters plus an optional fixed centre character. Building the first half lexicographically character-by-character allows us to calculate how many completions exist using the multinomial coefficient of remaining character frequencies. Because k is at most 10^6, whenever the number of completions exceeds k, we can cap our count at k without computing astronomical factorials, resolving each character decision in virtually O(1) time.
smallest-palindromic-rearrangement-ii.approach:
Tally character frequencies of s; identify the odd-frequency character (if any) as the centre character.
Divide all even character counts by 2 to get the multiset frequencies for constructing the first half of length m = n // 2.
Define a helper comb_capped(n, r, cap) that computes C(n, r) iteratively, immediately breaking out and returning cap if the running product exceeds cap.
Define a helper multiset_perms(counts, cap) that computes the multinomial coefficient product over non-zero counts, capping the total at cap.
Check if multiset_perms(half_counts, k) < k; if so, there aren't enough distinct palindromes, so return an empty string straight away.
Iterate through each position 0 to m - 1 of the first half.
For each candidate character 'a' through 'z' with non-zero frequency: temporarily decrement its count and compute ways = multiset_perms(remaining_counts, k).
If ways >= k, this candidate must be placed here; commit the character, decrement m, and break to the next position.
Otherwise, subtract ways from k, restore the candidate's frequency, and try the next letter.
Concatenate the chosen first half, the centre character (if n is odd), and the reversed first half to form the final result.

kth-smallest-element-in-a-bst.title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
kth-smallest-element-in-a-bst.insight: Because in-order traversal (Left, Root, Right) processes BST nodes in sorted ascending order, the k-th node popped is our target. By converting the traversal into an iterative stack-based approach, we can halt execution the moment we reach the k-th node, bounding time to O(h + k) and space to O(h).
kth-smallest-element-in-a-bst.approach:
Initialise an empty stack to track ancestor nodes and a pointer `curr = root`.
Loop while `curr` is not null or the `stack` is not empty.
Inner loop: push `curr` onto the stack and advance `curr = curr.left` until reaching the leftmost node.
Pop the top node from the stack — this is the current smallest unvisited node.
Decrement `k` by 1.
If `k` equals 0, return the popped node's value immediately.
Set `curr = popped.right` to start exploring the right subtree of the processed node, and repeat.
kth-smallest-element-in-a-bst.solution:
class Solution:
    def kthSmallest(self, root: Optional[TreeNode], k: int) -> int:
        stack = []
        curr = root
        
        while curr or stack:
            # Go as far left as possible
            while curr:
                stack.append(curr)
                curr = curr.left
            
            # Process the next smallest node
            curr = stack.pop()
            k -= 1
            if k == 0:
                return curr.val
            
            # Move to right child
            curr = curr.right
            
        return -1  # Unreachable given 1 <= k <= n

lfu-cache.title: LFU Cache
lfu-cache.insight: To evict in O(1), we need the minimum frequency and its oldest key immediately. We can store frequency buckets: a secondary map from frequency `f` to a doubly linked list of keys at that frequency. When an item's count increases from `f` to `f + 1`, we move it to the new bucket; if `f` was `min_freq` and is now empty, `min_freq` simply increments by 1. On a brand-new insert, `min_freq` always resets to 1.
lfu-cache.approach:
1. Define `key_to_val_freq` to store `key -> (value, freq)` and `freq_to_keys` mapping each `freq` to an `OrderedDict` (or doubly linked list).
2. Maintain `min_freq = 0`, tracking the smallest frequency currently present in the cache.
3. Write a helper `_update_freq(key)`: read its `val` and `freq`, remove `key` from `freq_to_keys[freq]`. If that list is empty and `min_freq == freq`, increment `min_freq` by 1. Append `key` to `freq_to_keys[freq + 1]` and update `key_to_val_freq`.
4. For `get(key)`: if `key` is absent, return -1. Otherwise, call `_update_freq(key)` and return its value.
5. For `put(key, value)`: if capacity <= 0, return early.
6. If `key` already exists: overwrite its value in `key_to_val_freq`, call `_update_freq(key)`, and return.
7. If `key` is new and cache is at capacity: pop the first (oldest) key from `freq_to_keys[min_freq]` and delete it from `key_to_val_freq`.
8. Insert `key` with value and freq 1 into `key_to_val_freq`, append it to `freq_to_keys[1]`, and set `min_freq = 1`.
lfu-cache.time: O(1) average for both get and put.

next-greater-element-iii.title: Next Greater Element III
next-greater-element-iii.insight: To make the number minimally larger, we must change a digit as far to the right as possible. We scan right-to-left to find the first dip where digits[i] < digits[i+1]. We then swap digits[i] with the smallest digit to its right that's strictly greater than it, and finally reverse everything to the right of index i to make that suffix as small as possible.
next-greater-element-iii.approach:
Convert the integer n into a mutable list of character digits.
Scan backwards from index len(digits) - 2 to find the first index i where digits[i] < digits[i + 1].
If no such index i exists, the digits are in descending order, so return -1.
Scan backwards again from the end to find the smallest index j such that digits[j] > digits[i].
Swap digits[i] and digits[j].
Reverse the suffix starting at index i + 1 up to the end to minimise the remaining digits.
Convert the digit list back to an integer.
Check if the resulting integer is <= 2^31 - 1; if so return it, otherwise return -1.
next-greater-element-iii.solution:
class Solution:
    def nextGreaterElement(self, n: int) -> int:
        digits = list(str(n))
        m = len(digits)
        
        # Step 1: Find the first decreasing digit from the right
        i = m - 2
        while i >= 0 and digits[i] >= digits[i + 1]:
            i -= 1
            
        # If no such digit, it's already the largest permutation
        if i < 0:
            return -1
            
        # Step 2: Find the smallest digit to the right of i that's greater than digits[i]
        j = m - 1
        while digits[j] <= digits[i]:
            j -= 1
            
        # Step 3: Swap them
        digits[i], digits[j] = digits[j], digits[i]
        
        # Step 4: Reverse the suffix after index i
        digits[i + 1:] = reversed(digits[i + 1:])
        
        ans = int(''.join(digits))
        
        # Must fit in 32-bit signed integer (up to 2^31 - 1)
        return ans if ans < (1 << 31) else -1

sort-characters-by-frequency.title: Sort Characters By Frequency
sort-characters-by-frequency.insight: The maximum possible frequency of any character is n (the length of the string). Instead of sorting unique characters in O(k log k), we can create an array of n + 1 buckets where index i holds all characters with frequency i. Scanning backwards from bucket n down to 1 produces the sorted string in strict O(n) time.
sort-characters-by-frequency.approach:
1. Count character frequencies in s using collections.Counter.
2. Initialise a list of empty lists `buckets` of size len(s) + 1.
3. Iterate through (char, freq) pairs and append char to `buckets[freq]`.
4. Initialise an empty list `res` to collect characters.
5. Loop through `buckets` backwards from index len(s) down to 1.
6. For each character in `buckets[freq]`, append `char * freq` to `res`.
7. Return `"".join(res)` as the final string.

partition-array-into-two-arrays-to-minim.title: Partition Array Into Two Arrays to Minimize Sum Difference
partition-array-into-two-arrays-to-minim.insight: Because n <= 15, 2^n is only 32,768. Splitting the array into two halves of size n lets us generate all 2^n subset sums for both halves bucketed by subset size k. For each left-half sum of size k, we need a right-half sum of size n - k that brings the combined sum closest to sum(nums) / 2, which we can find in O(log(2^n)) using binary search.
partition-array-into-two-arrays-to-minim.approach:
1. Calculate the total sum of `nums` and let `n = len(nums) // 2`.
2. Split `nums` into `left` and `right` halves, each having length `n`.
3. Create two lists of buckets (0 to n) for left and right: `left_sums[k]` stores all sums formed by picking `k` elements from `left`.
4. Iterate through all bitmasks from `0` to `2^n - 1` to populate subset sums and their element counts into both buckets.
5. Sort each bucket in `right_sums` to enable binary search.
6. Iterate `k` from 0 to n: for each `l_sum` in `left_sums[k]`, we need `n - k` elements from `right_sums`.
7. The ideal right sum is `(total / 2) - l_sum`. Use `bisect_left` on `right_sums[n - k]` to find the closest candidate.
8. Check both the element at the bisect index and the one immediately preceding it, updating the minimum absolute difference `abs(total - 2 * (l_sum + r_sum))`.
9. Return the overall minimum difference.
partition-array-into-two-arrays-to-minim.solution:
from bisect import bisect_left

class Solution:
    def minimumDifference(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        n = len(nums) // 2
        total = sum(nums)
        left, right = nums[:n], nums[n:]
        
        left_sums = [[] for _ in range(n + 1)]
        right_sums = [[] for _ in range(n + 1)]
        
        # Generate subset sums grouped by subset size
        for mask in range(1 << n):
            k = bin(mask).count('1')
            l_sum = sum(left[i] for i in range(n) if (mask & (1 << i)))
            r_sum = sum(right[i] for i in range(n) if (mask & (1 << i)))
            left_sums[k].append(l_sum)
            right_sums[k].append(r_sum)
            
        # Sort right buckets for binary search
        for k in range(n + 1):
            right_sums[k].sort()
            
        ans = float('inf')
        target = total / 2
        
        # Pair k elements from left with (n - k) from right
        for k in range(n + 1):
            r_candidates = right_sums[n - k]
            for l_sum in left_sums[k]:
                desired = target - l_sum
                idx = bisect_left(r_candidates, desired)
                
                # Check closest >= desired
                if idx < len(r_candidates):
                    ans = min(ans, abs(total - 2 * (l_sum + r_candidates[idx])))
                # Check closest < desired
                if idx > 0:
                    ans = min(ans, abs(total - 2 * (l_sum + r_candidates[idx - 1])))
                    
        return int(ans)

shortest-common-supersequence.title: Shortest Common Supersequence
shortest-common-supersequence.insight: Every shortest common supersequence has length `len(str1) + len(str2) - len(LCS)`. The characters in the Longest Common Subsequence are shared, so we only write them once. By building the standard 2D LCS grid `dp[i][j]`, we can backtrack from `(m, n)` back to `(0, 0)`: when characters match we write one copy and move diagonally; when they don't, we step in the direction that preserves the maximal LCS, taking the character from that string.
shortest-common-supersequence.approach:
Let `m = len(str1)` and `n = len(str2)`. Initialise a 2D table `dp` of size `(m + 1) x (n + 1)` with zeros.
Fill `dp[i][j]` with the length of the LCS of `str1[:i]` and `str2[:j]`: if `str1[i-1] == str2[j-1]`, `dp[i][j] = 1 + dp[i-1][j-1]`, else `max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])`.
Initialise two pointers `i = m`, `j = n` and an empty list `res` to collect characters in reverse.
While `i > 0` and `j > 0`: if `str1[i-1] == str2[j-1]`, append `str1[i-1]` and decrement both `i` and `j`.
Else, check if `dp[i-1][j] > dp[i][j-1]`: if so, append `str1[i-1]` and decrement `i`; otherwise, append `str2[j-1]` and decrement `j`.
After the loop, drain remaining characters: append `str1[i-1]` while `i > 0` (decrementing `i`), and `str2[j-1]` while `j > 0` (decrementing `j`).
Reverse `res` and join it into a string to return the result.

unique-paths-ii.title: Unique Paths II
unique-paths-ii.insight: Paths to (r, c) depend only on (r-1, c) and (r, c-1). An obstacle simply sets the path count to 0. Since we only need the value directly above and immediately to the left, we can collapse the full 2D table into a single 1D array representing the current row.
unique-paths-ii.approach:
1. Read grid dimensions m and n.
2. If the start cell grid[0][0] is 1, return 0 immediately.
3. Allocate a 1D DP array of length n filled with 0s, and set dp[0] = 1.
4. Iterate through each row r from 0 to m - 1.
5. For each column c from 0 to n - 1, check if grid[r][c] == 1.
6. If it is an obstacle, set dp[c] = 0 (no paths can pass through or carry over from above).
7. Else, if c > 0, add the left cell's paths to the current cell: dp[c] += dp[c - 1].
8. After processing all rows, dp[n - 1] holds the number of paths to the bottom-right corner.

remove-methods-from-project.title: Remove Methods From Project
remove-methods-from-project.insight: Suspicious methods are simply all nodes reachable from k. The condition that 'no method outside the group invokes any method within it' means there cannot exist a directed edge (u, v) where u is not suspicious and v is suspicious. We don't need reverse graphs or complex reachability queries; a simple check over all given edges suffices.
remove-methods-from-project.approach:
1. Build an adjacency list for the directed graph from the given invocations.
2. Run a standard BFS or DFS starting from node k to collect all reachable nodes into a set 'suspicious'.
3. Iterate through every edge [u, v] in the original invocations list.
4. If u is NOT in 'suspicious' and v IS in 'suspicious', then an external method invokes a suspicious one.
5. If such a cross-edge exists, we cannot remove anything, so immediately return all methods [0, 1, ..., n - 1].
6. If no such cross-edge exists across all edges, filter out the suspicious set and return all remaining nodes.

unique-morse-code-words.title: Unique Morse Code Words
unique-morse-code-words.insight: Morse conversion is purely deterministic: character `c` maps to `table[ord(c) - ord('a')]`. Since we only care about unique representations, feeding each concatenated Morse string directly into a hash set guarantees O(1) average deduplication and eliminates any pair-wise checks.
unique-morse-code-words.approach:
1. Define the 26-element Morse lookup array corresponding to letters 'a' through 'z'.
2. Initialise an empty hash set `seen` to store distinct transformed codes.
3. Loop through each word in the input list `words`.
4. For each word, map every character `c` to its Morse string via index `ord(c) - ord('a')`.
5. Concatenate these Morse snippets using `"".join(...)` to form the full transformation.
6. Add the concatenated transformation string into the `seen` set.
7. Return the length of `seen`.

range-sum-of-bst.title: Range Sum of BST
range-sum-of-bst.insight: Because this is a BST, if a node's value is strictly smaller than 'low', every value in its left subtree is also strictly smaller than 'low', so we can skip the left subtree entirely. Similarly, if a node's value is strictly greater than 'high', we can prune its right subtree. We only need to explore both subtrees when the current node's value lies strictly inside [low, high].
range-sum-of-bst.approach:
1. Define the base case: if the current node is null, return 0.
2. Check if node.val is strictly less than 'low': if so, discard the left subtree and recursively return the result of the right subtree.
3. Check if node.val is strictly greater than 'high': if so, discard the right subtree and recursively return the result of the left subtree.
4. If node.val is within [low, high], include node.val in the sum.
5. Recursively compute the sum from both left and right subtrees and add them to node.val.
6. Return the total combined sum back up the call stack.

smallest-divisible-digit-product-ii.title: Smallest Divisible Digit Product II
smallest-divisible-digit-product-ii.insight: Digits 1-9 only contribute prime factors 2, 3, 5, and 7. If t contains any other prime, it's impossible. For any remaining factor requirement (c2, c3, c5, c7), we can find the minimum number of digits needed to satisfy it (greedily packing factors into 9, 8, 6, 4, etc.). We then test prefix matches of num from longest to shortest: find the first index from the right where we can increment num[i] to a valid digit d, such that the remaining suffix length is at least the minimal digits required for the leftover factors, then pad with '1's and append the minimal digits sorted.
smallest-divisible-digit-product-ii.approach:
Factorise t into counts of 2, 3, 5, 7. If any other prime factor remains, return '-1'.
Write a helper function to compute the minimal digit string needed to satisfy prime requirements (c2, c3, c5, c7) by greedily picking 9s, 8s, 7s, 6s, 5s, 4s, 3s, 2s.
Find the first zero in num (if any); we can never match a prefix beyond the first zero.
First, check if num itself is valid (zero-free and digit product divisible by t). If so, return num directly.
Iterate suffix split point i backwards from len(num)-1 down to 0 (capped before the first zero).
At index i, try placing each digit d from int(num[i]) + 1 to 9.
Check if the remaining required factors can fit into the remaining len(num) - 1 - i slots.
If it fits, build the result: prefix[:i] + str(d) + '1' * padding + minimal_sorted_digits, and return it immediately.
If no same-length answer works, create a number of length max(len(num) + 1, min_digits_needed(t)), filled with leading '1's followed by the minimal digits for t.
smallest-divisible-digit-product-ii.solution:
class Solution:
    def smallestDivisibleDigitProduct(self, num: str, t: int) -> str:
        # Step 1: Factorise t into 2, 3, 5, 7
        c2 = c3 = c5 = c7 = 0
        for p, count_var in [(2, 'c2'), (3, 'c3'), (5, 'c5'), (7, 'c7')]:
            while t % p == 0:
                if p == 2: c2 += 1
                elif p == 3: c3 += 1
                elif p == 5: c5 += 1
                elif p == 7: c7 += 1
                t //= p
        if t > 1:
            return "-1"

        # Helper: count factor additions for a digit d (2..9)
        def get_factors(d: int):
            f2 = (d in (2, 6)) * 1 + (d == 4) * 2 + (d == 8) * 3
            f3 = (d in (3, 6)) * 1 + (d == 9) * 2
            f5 = 1 if d == 5 else 0
            f7 = 1 if d == 7 else 0
            return f2, f3, f5, f7

        # Helper: get minimal sorted digits to satisfy factor counts
        def get_min_digits(r2, r3, r5, r7):
            r2, r3, r5, r7 = max(0, r2), max(0, r3), max(0, r5), max(0, r7)
            res = []
            res.extend(['7'] * r7)
            res.extend(['5'] * r5)
            # Pack 3s into 9s
            n9 = r3 // 2
            r3 %= 2
            # Pack 2s into 8s
            n8 = r2 // 3
            r2 %= 3
            # Combine remaining 2 and 3 into 6 if possible
            if r3 == 1 and r2 == 2:
                # 3 and 4 -> 2 and 6 is worse, but 3*4=12 -> 2 and 6 is 2 digits; 2*6=12
                # Better: 9 and 8 packing handles most; remaining r3 <= 1, r2 <= 2
                res.extend(['2', '6'])
                r2, r3 = 0, 0
            elif r3 == 1 and r2 == 1:
                res.append('6')
                r2, r3 = 0, 0
            elif r3 == 1:
                res.append('3')
                r3 = 0
            elif r2 == 2:
                res.append('4')
                r2 = 0
            elif r2 == 1:
                res.append('2')
                r2 = 0
            res.extend(['8'] * n8)
            res.extend(['9'] * n9)
            res.sort()
            return res

        n = len(num)
        # Check if num itself has a zero
        first_zero = num.find('0')
        max_prefix = first_zero if first_zero != -1 else n

        # Compute prefix factor prefix sums
        pref2, pref3, pref5, pref7 = [0] * (n + 1), [0] * (n + 1), [0] * (n + 1), [0] * (n + 1)
        for i in range(max_prefix):
            d = int(num[i])
            f2, f3, f5, f7 = get_factors(d)
            pref2[i+1] = pref2[i] + f2
            pref3[i+1] = pref3[i] + f3
            pref5[i+1] = pref5[i] + f5
            pref7[i+1] = pref7[i] + f7

        # Case 0: num itself is zero-free and valid
        if first_zero == -1 and pref2[n] >= c2 and pref3[n] >= c3 and pref5[n] >= c5 and pref7[n] >= c7:
            return num

        # Case 1: same length, branch from index i
        for i in range(max_prefix - 1, -1, -1):
            cur_d = int(num[i])
            for d in range(cur_d + 1, 10):
                f2, f3, f5, f7 = get_factors(d)
                rem2 = c2 - (pref2[i] + f2)
                rem3 = c3 - (pref3[i] + f3)
                rem5 = c5 - (pref5[i] + f5)
                rem7 = c7 - (pref7[i] + f7)
                min_digits = get_min_digits(rem2, rem3, rem5, rem7)
                rem_len = n - 1 - i
                if len(min_digits) <= rem_len:
                    padding = ['1'] * (rem_len - len(min_digits))
                    return num[:i] + str(d) + ''.join(padding) + ''.join(min_digits)

        # Case 2: longer length required
        min_digits = get_min_digits(c2, c3, c5, c7)
        target_len = max(n + 1, len(min_digits))
        padding = ['1'] * (target_len - len(min_digits))
        return ''.join(padding) + ''.join(min_digits)

backspace-string-compare.title: Backspace String Compare
backspace-string-compare.insight: Working forwards is tricky without extra space because a '#' deletes a character that's already in the past. If we walk backwards from the end, a '#' acts as a credit to delete the *next* valid character we encounter. By tracking our 'skip' count going backwards, we can resolve characters on the fly and compare them one by one without storing anything.
backspace-string-compare.approach:
Initialise pointer i at s.length() - 1 and pointer j at t.length() - 1.
Initialise skip counters skipS = 0 and skipT = 0.
Loop while i >= 0 or j >= 0 (since one string might exhaust before the other).
Find the next valid character in s: if s[i] is '#', increment skipS and decrement i; else if skipS > 0, decrement skipS and decrement i; otherwise, break.
Repeat the exact same skip logic for t using pointer j and skipT.
Compare the found characters: if both pointers are in bounds (i >= 0 and j >= 0) and s[i] != t[j], return False.
If one pointer is in bounds and the other is out of bounds (one exhausted, the other has a real character left), return False.
Decrement both i and j to move past the compared characters and continue.
If the loop finishes without mismatches, return True.

fruits-into-baskets-iii.title: Fruits Into Baskets III
fruits-into-baskets-iii.insight: We need the *first* index j where capacity >= fruit. If we maintain a segment tree over basket capacities storing range maximums, we can check if the left child's maximum is >= fruit; if so, the answer is guaranteed to be in the left subtree, otherwise we go right. Once found, we set that leaf to -1 (used) and update ancestors in O(log n).
fruits-into-baskets-iii.approach:
Initialise a segment tree of size 4n to store the maximum basket capacity in each subtree.
Build the segment tree recursively with the initial values from baskets.
Maintain an unplaced fruit counter initialised to 0.
Iterate through each fruit in fruits from left to right.
Check the root of the segment tree: if tree[1] < fruit, no valid basket exists, so increment unplaced and continue.
Otherwise, recursively query/update down the tree: if the left child's maximum is >= fruit, descend into the left child; else descend into the right child.
Upon reaching the leaf at index j, set its capacity to -1 (marking it consumed) and update maximums on the way back up.
After processing all fruits, return the unplaced count.

check-if-object-instance-of-class.title: Check if Object Instance of Class
check-if-object-instance-of-class.insight: The built-in operator fails on primitives because they are not boxed objects in memory. If we guard against null/undefined and then wrap the value into an object using Object(obj), we can traverse the prototype chain via Object.getPrototypeOf() and compare directly with classFunction.prototype.
check-if-object-instance-of-class.approach:
1. Check if obj is null or undefined; if so, immediately return false.
2. Check if classFunction is a function or object with a valid prototype; if not, return false.
3. Wrap obj using Object(obj) to ensure primitives are boxed into their wrapper objects.
4. Initialise a pointer curr to Object.getPrototypeOf(Object(obj)).
5. Loop while curr is not null.
6. If curr strictly equals classFunction.prototype, return true.
7. Update curr = Object.getPrototypeOf(curr) to move one step up the chain.
8. If the loop terminates at null, return false.

substring-with-concatenation-of-all-word.title: Substring with Concatenation of All Words
substring-with-concatenation-of-all-word.insight: Because every word has fixed length L, any valid match aligns to word boundaries offset by some i in range(L). By fixing an offset i and stepping in strides of L, we turn this into a classic sliding window where words enter on the right and leave on the left.
substring-with-concatenation-of-all-word.approach:
1. Calculate word_len L and total_words count M. If len(s) < M * L, return empty list.
2. Build target_count frequency map of words.
3. Loop offset i from 0 to L - 1 to cover all possible word alignment phases.
4. For each offset, maintain left = i, words_matched = 0, and a seen frequency map.
5. Advance right from i to len(s) - L in strides of L, extracting current_word = s[right:right+L].
6. If current_word is in target_count, increment seen[current_word] and words_matched.
7. If seen[current_word] > target_count[current_word], slide left forward by L-steps, decrementing seen counts until seen[current_word] <= target_count[current_word].
8. If words_matched == M, append left to results, then advance left by L to search for subsequent matches.
9. If current_word is not in target_count, reset seen, words_matched = 0, and set left = right + L.
substring-with-concatenation-of-all-word.solution:
from collections import Counter, defaultdict

class Solution:
    def findSubstring(self, s: str, words: list[str]) -> list[int]:
        if not s or not words:
            return []
        
        w_len = len(words[0])
        num_words = len(words)
        total_len = w_len * num_words
        n = len(s)
        
        if n < total_len:
            return []
        
        target = Counter(words)
        ans = []
        
        # We only need w_len different starting offsets
        for offset in range(w_len):
            left = offset
            seen = defaultdict(int)
            matched = 0
            
            for right in range(offset, n - w_len + 1, w_len):
                word = s[right:right + w_len]
                
                if word in target:
                    seen[word] += 1
                    matched += 1
                    
                    # If word count exceeds target, shrink from left
                    while seen[word] > target[word]:
                        left_word = s[left:left + w_len]
                        seen[left_word] -= 1
                        matched -= 1
                        left += w_len
                    
                    # Valid window found
                    if matched == num_words:
                        ans.append(left)
                else:
                    # Invalid word: flush window and reset left past this word
                    seen.clear()
                    matched = 0
                    left = right + w_len
                    
        return ans

remove-k-digits.title: Remove K Digits
remove-k-digits.insight: Leftmost digits carry the highest place-value weight, so replacing any digit with a smaller adjacent successor immediately yields a smaller overall number. A monotonic increasing stack lets us efficiently discard local peaks as soon as a smaller digit arrives, using up our budget of k removals greedily.
remove-k-digits.approach:
1. Initialise an empty list `stack` to store the digits of the resulting number.
2. Iterate through each digit in `num` from left to right.
3. While `k > 0`, `stack` is not empty, and the top digit of `stack` is strictly greater than the current digit, pop from `stack` and decrement `k`.
4. Append the current digit to `stack`.
5. After the loop, if `k > 0` (e.g. for already sorted numbers like '12345'), pop the remaining `k` elements from the end of `stack` using slicing `stack[:-k]`.
6. Join `stack` to form a string and strip leading zeros using `.lstrip('0')`.
7. Return the stripped string, or `'0'` if the result is empty.
remove-k-digits.solution:
class Solution:
    def removeKdigits(self, num: str, k: int) -> str:
        stack = []
        
        for digit in num:
            # Greedily remove larger digits before the current smaller one
            while k > 0 and stack and stack[-1] > digit:
                stack.pop()
                k -= 1
            stack.append(digit)
        
        # If k remains, drop digits from the end (monotonic ascending tail)
        final_digits = stack[:-k] if k > 0 else stack
        
        # Strip leading zeros and handle empty string fallback
        result = "".join(final_digits).lstrip("0")
        return result if result else "0"

find-minimum-in-rotated-sorted-array-ii.title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array II
find-minimum-in-rotated-sorted-array-ii.insight: Comparing nums[mid] with nums[right] tells us which side the drop occurs on. If nums[mid] > nums[right], the minimum has to be strictly to the right. If nums[mid] < nums[right], the right half is sorted, so the minimum is at mid or to its left. Crucially, when nums[mid] == nums[right], we can't tell which side the pivot is on (consider [3,1,3,3] vs [3,3,1,3]), but because nums[right] is duplicated at nums[mid], we can safely discard nums[right] with right -= 1 without losing the answer.
find-minimum-in-rotated-sorted-array-ii.approach:
1. Initialise pointers left = 0 and right = len(nums) - 1.
2. Loop whilst left < right.
3. Compute mid = left + (right - left) // 2 to prevent integer overflow.
4. If nums[mid] > nums[right], the inflection point is in the right half, so set left = mid + 1.
5. Else if nums[mid] < nums[right], the minimum is at mid or in the left half, so set right = mid.
6. Else (nums[mid] == nums[right]), we cannot determine the half, so safely decrement right -= 1.
7. When left == right, the loop terminates and left points directly at the minimum element.
8. Return nums[left].
find-minimum-in-rotated-sorted-array-ii.time: O(log n) average, O(n) worst case

basic-calculator-ii.title: Basic Calculator II
